1.6

Testing ML / Data Code

highverified
Roles: mle, aie

Topic overview

Testing data and machine-learning software requires more than checking a few expected numbers. A useful suite separates deterministic transformation behavior, data contracts, numerical properties, model behavior, component integration, and end-to-end system paths. It also controls nondeterminism without pretending stochastic systems are bit-for-bit stable. This chapter develops a risk-based test strategy using plain assertions and pytest concepts: arrange-act-assert, fixtures with scoped cleanup, parametrization, temporary resources, monkeypatching at the lookup site, approximate comparisons, property and metamorphic checks, golden artifacts, and model regression tests. You will learn why test data should be tiny but adversarial, how to avoid leakage between tests, how to choose tolerances, and how to keep slow or flaky external dependencies out of unit tests. The worked example tests a normalization transform against shape, finiteness, constant-column, and training-statistic invariants. The production perspective connects local tests to schema validation, shadow evaluation, canaries, monitoring, rollback, and incident reproduction. The aim is evidence about failure risk, not a high coverage percentage detached from behavior.

Prerequisites

  • python-data-structures
  • numpy-vectorization
  • pandas-core

Learning objectives

  • Map risks in data, numerical, model, and system behavior to the cheapest reliable test layer.
  • Use fixtures, parametrization, dependency seams, approximate assertions, and metamorphic properties without shared-state leakage.
  • Design regression and integration checks that remain deterministic, interpretable, and useful during deployment and rollback.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Test ML and data systems in layers: unit-test deterministic transforms and edge cases; validate schemas and invariants on representative data; test numerical properties with justified tolerances; regression-test model outputs or metrics on frozen slices; and integration-test serialization, feature parity, and serving paths. Control randomness and external dependencies, but do not replace production monitoring. A good test names the risk it catches and fails with enough evidence to diagnose it.

What you must know

  • Test risks, not implementation trivia
  • Tiny adversarial fixtures
  • Approximate numerical invariants
  • Separate code, data, and model checks
  • Monitoring covers what tests cannot

Why this matters

Data code often runs successfully while producing incorrect data. Models can satisfy shape checks while degrading a minority slice. Serialization or preprocessing differences can make offline evaluation irrelevant to serving. A suite therefore needs semantic assertions: row and key contracts, absence of leakage, finiteness, monotonicity, invariance, and metric thresholds with uncertainty. Interviews probe testing because production ML combines conventional software failure with data drift and statistical variation. A precise answer distinguishes deterministic tests from noisy evaluation and explains why tests before deployment and monitoring after deployment are complementary controls.

Intuition

A test is a small experiment against a claim. Unit tests isolate a deterministic claim; integration tests check contracts between parts; model evaluations estimate behavior over a dataset; monitoring observes the real environment. Use the narrowest experiment that can falsify the risk. A tiny table containing a duplicate key, null, unseen category, boundary timestamp, and constant column often teaches more than a large random fixture whose failure is hard to understand.

A risk-based test portfolio

Unit tests cover pure parsing, feature calculations, shape transformations, loss helpers, and decision rules. They should be fast, deterministic, and local. Contract tests validate interfaces: schema, dtype, units, nullability, ordering, model signature, and serialized format. Integration tests exercise real boundaries such as database adapters, object storage, a feature service, or model loading. A small number of end-to-end tests verify the critical path in an environment close to production.

Data validation is not simply another unit assertion. It evaluates a dataset or batch against constraints and distribution expectations. Model regression tests use a frozen dataset and artifact to detect unintended changes in predictions, metrics, calibration, latency, or size. They should not freeze improvement: thresholds and reviewed golden changes distinguish intended updates from accidents. Slice tests expose failures hidden by an aggregate metric.

Prioritize by impact, likelihood, and detectability. Test leakage, label alignment, join cardinality, preprocessing parity, and rollback before cosmetic formatting. Coverage can reveal unexecuted code but does not prove behavioral adequacy. Mutation testing or deliberate fault injection can show whether assertions actually notice a broken branch. Every production incident should yield the cheapest reproducible test or monitor that would have detected it.

Fixtures, parametrization, and dependency control

pytest discovers test functions and rewrites plain `assert` statements to provide useful failure detail. Parametrization runs one behavior across explicit cases, making boundaries visible without copy-paste. Parameters are passed as-is, so mutable values can leak changes between cases; create fresh objects when mutation is part of the test. Give cases readable IDs so failures identify the scenario.

Fixtures provide explicit setup dependencies and can yield a value, then perform teardown. Scope controls lifetime: function scope maximizes isolation; broader scopes can speed expensive stable setup but increase coupling and contamination risk. Prefer small composable fixtures over a global environment. Temporary-path fixtures avoid collisions, and cleanup must run on failures. Use factories when each test needs multiple independently configured objects.

Monkeypatch the name looked up by the code under test, not the function's original definition in an unrelated module. Better still, inject clocks, random generators, clients, and repositories through explicit seams. Fake deterministic boundaries locally; keep separate contract/integration tests against real services. An over-mocked test can pass while components cannot work together. Assert observable results and important interactions, not every internal call sequence, so refactoring does not create noise.

Numerical, stochastic, and model behavior tests

Floating-point results should usually be compared with absolute and relative tolerances tied to scale, dtype, and algorithm, not an arbitrary large epsilon. Assert shape, dtype, finiteness, and domain bounds before value closeness. Test constant inputs, empty permitted inputs, large magnitude, missing values, and near-boundary decisions. Numerical algorithms often have properties stronger than fixtures: normalized probabilities sum to one, a distance is nonnegative and symmetric, a permutation-equivariant transform changes correspondingly, or increasing a threshold cannot increase the accepted set.

Property-based tests generate inputs across a domain; metamorphic tests verify relationships when an exact oracle is difficult. They supplement carefully selected examples. Fix a random seed for reproducibility, pass an explicit generator, and store failure seeds. A fixed seed does not make GPU kernels, distributed reductions, or external models universally deterministic. Define acceptable variability and separate a deterministic smoke check from a statistical evaluation repeated over enough examples or seeds.

Model tests can verify signature, serialization round-trip, preprocessing parity, prediction range, known examples, slice metrics, and comparison with an approved baseline. A single metric threshold may be noisy or encourage overfitting to the test set. Record dataset version, confidence or uncertainty, and multiple safety-critical metrics. Never use the test suite's frozen evaluation set to repeatedly tune the model without accounting for adaptive overfitting.

Maintaining tests across the ML lifecycle

A test should be independent, deterministic within its stated contract, and diagnostic. Name the behavior and scenario. Arrange only the data needed, perform one meaningful action, and assert invariants with messages or rich comparisons. Avoid time sleeps, live network calls, global random state, and dependence on test order. Quarantine is not a permanent solution for flakiness; classify whether the cause is a race, nondeterminism, environment, timeout, or an invalid assertion and fix the source.

Golden files are useful for complex structured outputs when reviewed diffs are meaningful. Normalize volatile IDs and timestamps and avoid blindly accepting snapshots. Large model artifacts do not belong in every unit test; use a tiny deterministic substitute plus separate artifact compatibility tests. Mark slow, GPU, and external integration suites and run them at an appropriate CI stage. Cache dependencies without sharing mutable outputs.

Deployment adds checks tests cannot simulate completely: shadow comparisons, canary metrics, feature distribution and missingness monitoring, latency and error budgets, human review, and rollback drills. Link a release to code, data, feature, configuration, and model versions so a regression is reproducible. Alerts require ownership and playbooks. Testing reduces known risk; monitoring detects environmental change and unknown failure modes.

Math / formal view

For floating results x and y, a common closeness rule is |x-y| ≤ atol + rtol·|y|, with tolerances justified by dtype and scale. For a metric estimate p over n independent binary outcomes, sampling uncertainty is on the order of sqrt(p(1-p)/n); therefore tiny evaluation sets cannot support narrow regression thresholds.

Verify a normalization component beyond one expected array

Setup

A transformer fits per-feature mean and scale on training rows, maps constant columns safely, then is serialized for serving.

Use a tiny non-square matrix with one varying and one constant column. Assert fitted statistic shapes, unchanged sample/feature shape, finite output, zero mean and unit standard deviation only for the varying training feature, and zeros for the centered constant feature. Transform a validation row using stored training statistics and assert fit state does not change. Parametrize float32 and float64 with appropriate tolerances. Round-trip the artifact and compare outputs. Add invalid-shape and non-finite-policy cases.

Conclusion

The suite checks mathematical properties, state ownership, leakage prevention, dtype behavior, error paths, and serving compatibility rather than one happy-path snapshot.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Test a numerical transformer with example, property, error-path, state, and round-trip assertions.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
class Standardizer:
    def fit(self, X):
        import numpy as np
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        if X.ndim != 2:
            raise ValueError('expected 2D input')
        self.mean_ = X.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
        scale = X.std(axis=0, keepdims=True)
        self.scale_ = np.where(scale == 0, 1.0, scale)
        return self
    def transform(self, X):
        import numpy as np
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        if X.ndim != 2 or X.shape[1] != self.mean_.shape[1]:
            raise ValueError('feature mismatch')
        return (X - self.mean_) / self.scale_
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1., 5.], [3., 5.], [5., 5.]])
transformer = Standardizer().fit(X)
Z = transformer.transform(X)
validation = transformer.transform([[7., 5.]])
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Run fast checks per change, version golden datasets and artifacts, separate environment suites, record seeds and tolerances, and combine pre-release regression with canary monitoring and rollback.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert Z.shape == X.shape
assert np.isfinite(Z).all()
assert np.allclose(Z[:, 0].mean(), 0.0)
assert np.allclose(Z[:, 0].std(), 1.0)
assert np.allclose(Z[:, 1], 0.0)
before = transformer.mean_.copy()
transformer.transform([[9., 5.]])
assert np.array_equal(before, transformer.mean_)
try:
    transformer.transform([[1., 2., 3.]])
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError('feature mismatch must fail')

Common mistakes

  • High line coverage means the ML system is well tested.

    Coverage only reports execution. It does not prove assertions cover leakage, data contracts, numerical properties, model slices, or integration boundaries.

  • Set one global seed and every result becomes deterministic.

    Seeds control specific random streams; parallel hardware, libraries, data order, and external services can remain nondeterministic.

  • Mock every dependency in unit tests and integration is covered.

    Mocks can drift from real contracts. Use local fakes for speed plus contract and integration tests against actual boundaries.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do you test a model when exact predictions legitimately change?

    Test stable invariants and signatures, then compare approved metrics and slices on versioned data with justified tolerances or uncertainty rather than exact arrays everywhere.

  • Where should monkeypatch be applied?

    Patch the symbol where the code under test looks it up. Prefer explicit dependency injection when the dependency is part of the design.

  • What is a metamorphic test?

    It checks a known relationship between transformed inputs and outputs when an exact expected result is hard to specify, such as permutation invariance or monotonicity.

Production / system-design connection

Gate releases with fast deterministic tests, schema and lineage checks, artifact compatibility, frozen-slice evaluation, and limited end-to-end paths. Separate slow/GPU suites while ensuring they run before release. Store failure seeds and version every input artifact. After deployment, use shadow or canary comparisons, monitor data and model slices, enforce latency/error budgets, and rehearse rollback. Convert incidents into regression tests and operational monitors with clear owners.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    Why should floating-point tests use both relative and absolute tolerances?

    Show solution

    Relative tolerance scales with magnitude, while absolute tolerance handles expected values near zero where a purely relative bound becomes ineffective.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Design three cases for a many-to-one feature join.

    Show solution

    Include a normal match, an unmatched left record with explicit missing policy, and a duplicated right key that must fail cardinality validation.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A unit test patches `requests.get`, but the module imported `get` directly and still calls the network. Why?

    Show solution

    The module looks up its own imported name. Patch that lookup site or inject a client into the function.

2.1

Big-O Time & Space Complexity

highsummary
Roles: ds, mle, de, aie
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Big-O describes how runtime or memory grows with input size. I use it to compare algorithms asymptotically, while remembering constants, cache behavior and real input sizes still matter in practice.

What you must know

  • Know O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²).
  • Distinguish worst, average and amortized complexity.
  • Analyze both time and memory.

Why this matters

Big-O Time & Space Complexity appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Know O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²).

Deep explanation

Big-O describes how runtime or memory grows with input size. I use it to compare algorithms asymptotically, while remembering constants, cache behavior and real input sizes still matter in practice. Distinguish worst, average and amortized complexity. Analyze both time and memory. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Sorting ten million rows with an O(n log n) algorithm is usually viable; an accidental nested O(n²) comparison can become catastrophic.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
  • Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.

Likely follow-ups

  • What assumptions does Big-O Time & Space Complexity make?
  • How would you validate or debug Big-O Time & Space Complexity in practice?

Production / system-design connection

3.1

SQL Joins

very highsummary
Roles: ds, de, mle, da
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

INNER JOIN returns matching rows; LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left side and fills unmatched right-side columns with NULL; FULL OUTER JOIN keeps rows from both sides. Choose based on what records must survive the join.

What you must know

  • Join keys
  • Duplicate amplification
  • NULL behavior
  • Many-to-many joins

Why this matters

Joins test whether you understand relational grain, keys and duplicate amplification—not just SQL syntax. They are central to feature building, analytics and ETL.

Intuition

A join decides which rows survive when two tables are connected by a key. Before writing SQL, state the grain of each table and whether the key is one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many.

Deep explanation

INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows. LEFT JOIN preserves every left-side row and fills unmatched right columns with NULL. FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both sides. A many-to-many join multiplies rows, which is often the source of silent metric inflation. Join predicates belong in ON when they define matching logic; filters in WHERE can accidentally turn a LEFT JOIN into INNER-like behavior by removing NULL matches.

Worked example

customers has one row per customer while orders has many rows per customer. Joining them creates one row per order, not one row per customer. If you later average a customer-level feature without re-aggregating, heavy buyers are overrepresented.

Quick code / pseudocode

SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

Common mistakes

  • Ignoring table grain and creating duplicate amplification.
  • Filtering right-table columns in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN and unintentionally dropping unmatched rows.
  • Joining on non-unique or dirty keys without checking cardinality.

Likely follow-ups

  • INNER vs LEFT JOIN?
  • What happens in a many-to-many join?
  • How do NULLs behave in joins?
  • How would you detect duplicate amplification?

Production / system-design connection

In feature pipelines, validate join cardinality, row counts and uniqueness before/after joins. Point-in-time joins are essential to prevent temporal leakage.

3.2

GROUP BY, HAVING & Aggregation

highsummary
Roles: ds, de, mle, da
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

GROUP BY changes the grain of the result by aggregating rows into groups. WHERE filters before aggregation; HAVING filters after aggregation.

What you must know

  • Row grain
  • COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)
  • WHERE vs HAVING
  • Conditional aggregation

Why this matters

Aggregation tests row-grain reasoning and is ubiquitous in analytics and feature engineering.

Intuition

GROUP BY collapses rows sharing group keys. WHERE filters input rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregate values exist.

Deep explanation

Every selected non-aggregated column must be functionally compatible with the group grain. COUNT(*) counts rows while COUNT(column) ignores NULL. Conditional aggregation with CASE computes multiple metrics in one pass. Be careful that joins before aggregation may duplicate facts and inflate sums.

Worked example

To find customers with at least five completed orders, filter completed rows in WHERE, group by customer, then HAVING COUNT(*)>=5.

Quick code / pseudocode

SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n_orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status='completed'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5;

Common mistakes

  • Using WHERE with an aggregate expression instead of HAVING.
  • Forgetting COUNT(column) ignores NULL.
  • Aggregating after a duplicate-amplifying join without checking grain.

Likely follow-ups

  • WHERE vs HAVING?
  • COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)?
  • How do you do conditional aggregation?
  • When would a window function be better?

Production / system-design connection

Feature pipelines should document output grain and validate counts/sums against source totals so join/aggregation mistakes are caught early.

3.3

Window Functions

very highsummary
Roles: ds, de, mle, da
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Window functions compute values across related rows without collapsing them. Common examples are ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD and running aggregates using OVER(PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...).

What you must know

  • Window vs GROUP BY
  • Partition and ordering
  • Ranking
  • Rolling metrics

Why this matters

Window functions are a common SQL interview discriminator because they solve ranking, lag/lead and rolling calculations without collapsing row-level detail.

Intuition

GROUP BY reduces many rows into one row per group. A window function keeps the original rows but lets each row look across a defined set of neighboring rows.

Deep explanation

The OVER clause defines the window. PARTITION BY resets calculations by group; ORDER BY defines sequence; a frame such as ROWS BETWEEN controls which ordered rows contribute. ROW_NUMBER assigns unique positions, RANK leaves gaps after ties, DENSE_RANK does not. LAG/LEAD access prior/future rows and are useful for temporal features.

Worked example

To find each customer’s latest order, assign ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) and keep row_number=1. This avoids a separate aggregate-plus-join pattern.

Quick code / pseudocode

SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT o.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER(
           PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC
         ) AS rn
  FROM orders o
) x
WHERE rn = 1;

Common mistakes

  • Confusing PARTITION BY with GROUP BY.
  • Ignoring tie behavior between ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK.
  • Using LAG/LEAD without an explicit, meaningful ordering.

Likely follow-ups

  • ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK?
  • How do you calculate a running average?
  • Window function vs GROUP BY?
  • What is a window frame?

Production / system-design connection

Window functions are useful in feature generation, deduplication and event sequencing, but large partitions/orderings can be expensive; inspect execution plans and partition strategies.

3.4

CTEs & Subqueries

mediumsummary
Roles: ds, de, mle, da
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

CTEs make complex SQL easier to reason about by naming intermediate results. They are often used to structure transformations before the final query.

What you must know

  • Readability
  • Recursive CTE concept
  • Optimization depends on database
  • Avoid unnecessary nesting

Why this matters

CTEs and subqueries test how you structure multi-step SQL and reason about readability versus optimizer behavior.

Intuition

A subquery nests a query inside another expression. A CTE names an intermediate query so complex logic reads like staged transformations.

Deep explanation

CTEs improve organization and can be recursive. Modern optimizers may inline them, but materialization behavior is database/version specific. Correlated subqueries reference outer rows and can be expensive if not optimized. EXISTS is often a clear way to express “does any related row exist?” without duplicate joins.

Worked example

Use a CTE to aggregate order spend per customer, then join that one-row-per-customer result to customer attributes. This makes grain explicit.

Quick code / pseudocode

WITH spend AS (
 SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) total
 FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.customer_id, s.total
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN spend s USING(customer_id);

Common mistakes

  • Assuming a CTE always materializes or is always faster.
  • Using SELECT * in deeply nested transformations and losing schema clarity.
  • Using correlated subqueries without checking the execution plan.

Likely follow-ups

  • CTE vs subquery?
  • What is a correlated subquery?
  • EXISTS vs IN?
  • What is a recursive CTE?

Production / system-design connection

Prefer maintainable SQL with explicit grain/columns; performance decisions should come from query plans and realistic data, not blanket rules about CTEs.

3.5

Transactions & Indexes

mediumsummary
Roles: de, mle, da
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Transactions group operations into an atomic unit with ACID guarantees. Indexes speed reads by maintaining an auxiliary search structure, but they consume storage and make writes more expensive.

What you must know

  • ACID
  • Commit/rollback
  • B-tree intuition
  • Read/write trade-off

Why this matters

Transactions protect correctness under concurrent updates; indexes trade storage/write cost for faster access. Both matter in ML/data applications with databases.

Intuition

A transaction groups changes so they behave as one logical unit. An index is an auxiliary search structure that helps find rows without scanning the whole table.

Deep explanation

ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability. Isolation levels trade concurrency for protection against anomalies. B-tree indexes are common for equality/range queries; composite index column order matters. Indexes speed reads but consume storage and slow writes/maintenance. An index cannot rescue every query—low-selectivity filters or functions can still scan heavily.

Worked example

A service that writes prediction + audit metadata should commit both together. An index on (customer_id, event_time) can accelerate recent-history lookup for one customer.

Quick code / pseudocode

BEGIN;
UPDATE inventory SET qty=qty-1 WHERE sku='A';
INSERT INTO audit_log(event) VALUES('reserve A');
COMMIT;

CREATE INDEX idx_events_customer_time ON events(customer_id,event_time);

Common mistakes

  • Adding indexes to every column.
  • Assuming transactions eliminate all concurrency anomalies at every isolation level.
  • Ignoring index order in composite indexes.

Likely follow-ups

  • What does ACID mean?
  • Clustered vs non-clustered concept?
  • When does an index hurt?
  • What is a deadlock?

Production / system-design connection

Monitor slow queries, lock contention and write amplification. Schema/index changes need migration plans and load testing on realistic cardinalities.

3.6

Stored Procedures & Data Pipelines

mediumsummary
Roles: de, ds, da
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Stored procedures package database-side logic such as selection, joins and transformations. In data pipelines, orchestration tools can call these procedures and move their outputs to downstream stages.

What you must know

  • Database-side logic
  • Parameters
  • Transactions
  • Separation from orchestration

Why this matters

Stored procedures appear in enterprise data systems and are relevant when explaining SQL-centric ETL experience.

Intuition

A stored procedure packages database-side SQL logic behind a callable name so applications or orchestrators can execute a consistent transformation close to the data.

Deep explanation

Procedures can contain parameterized queries, branching, temporary tables, transactions and error handling. Benefits include centralized logic and reduced data movement; drawbacks include vendor coupling, harder versioning/testing and hidden business logic if poorly managed. Orchestrators such as ADF can call procedures as pipeline activities.

Worked example

A new user story requires data from several tables. A procedure joins/filters them into the required shape; ADF triggers the procedure and moves the output to the next pipeline stage.

Quick code / pseudocode

-- conceptual
CREATE PROCEDURE get_customer_features @as_of DATE AS
SELECT ...
FROM a JOIN b ON ...
WHERE event_date <= @as_of;

Common mistakes

  • Putting every business rule into opaque database procedures with no version control.
  • Building dynamic SQL unsafely from user input.
  • Confusing a stored procedure with the orchestration pipeline itself.

Likely follow-ups

  • Stored procedure vs view?
  • Why execute logic in the database?
  • How would ADF call a procedure?
  • How do you debug a failing pipeline activity?

Production / system-design connection

Keep SQL/procedure definitions in source control, test with representative data, log parameters/run IDs and separate database logic from orchestration concerns.

5.1

Vectors, Matrices & Dot Products

very highsummary
Roles: all, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A vector represents an ordered set of features or a direction; a matrix represents a linear transformation or collection of vectors. The dot product measures alignment and is the core operation behind linear models, attention scores and neural layers.

What you must know

  • Geometric and algebraic views
  • Matrix multiplication as composition
  • Dot product and similarity
  • Shapes matter

Why this matters

Vectors and matrices are the language of embeddings, linear models, neural networks, PCA, attention and almost every numerical ML implementation.

Intuition

A vector is an ordered list representing a point, direction or feature set. A matrix is a collection of vectors and can be viewed as a linear transformation that rotates, scales, projects or mixes coordinates.

Deep explanation

The dot product measures alignment and also computes weighted sums. Matrix multiplication composes linear transformations and requires inner dimensions to match. Norms measure vector magnitude. Rank tells how many independent directions a matrix contains. In ML, a batch is often a matrix X with rows as samples and columns as features; a linear layer computes XW+b.

Math / formal view

Dot product: x·w = Σ_i x_i w_i Matrix product: C_ij = Σ_k A_ik B_kj L2 norm: ||x||₂ = sqrt(Σ_i x_i²)

Worked example

If X has shape (batch, 10) and W has shape (10, 32), then XW has shape (batch, 32). Each output feature is a dot product between the input and one column of W.

Quick code / pseudocode

import numpy as np
X=np.random.randn(64,10)
W=np.random.randn(10,32)
Y=X@W
print(Y.shape)  # (64, 32)

Common mistakes

  • Mixing elementwise multiplication with matrix multiplication.
  • Ignoring tensor shapes during architecture explanations.
  • Saying cosine similarity and dot product are identical without normalization assumptions.

Likely follow-ups

  • What does a dot product mean geometrically?
  • What is matrix rank?
  • Why does matrix multiplication order matter?
  • How are embeddings compared?

Production / system-design connection

Shape reasoning prevents many silent bugs in deep learning, vector search and batched inference. Log/validate tensor dimensions at system boundaries.

5.2

Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors & SVD

highsummary
Roles: ds, mle, aie, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Eigenvectors are directions preserved by a linear transformation up to scaling. SVD decomposes any matrix into orthogonal directions and singular values, making it useful for compression, PCA intuition and low-rank approximation.

What you must know

  • Eigen equation Av=λv
  • SVD works for rectangular matrices
  • Low-rank approximation
  • Connection to PCA

Why this matters

Eigenvectors/SVD underpin PCA, low-rank approximation, conditioning and many representation/compression methods.

Intuition

An eigenvector is a direction a square matrix transforms without changing direction, only scale. SVD decomposes any matrix into orthogonal input/output directions with nonnegative strengths.

Deep explanation

For square A, Av=λv. SVD exists for any m×n matrix: A=UΣVᵀ. Singular values rank directions by how strongly the transformation acts. Truncating small singular values gives the best low-rank approximation under common norms and reveals effective dimensionality. For symmetric covariance matrices, PCA eigenvectors correspond to right singular vectors of centered data.

Math / formal view

Av=λv A=UΣVᵀ Rank-k approximation: A_k=U_k Σ_k V_kᵀ

Worked example

A dataset with 100 correlated features may have most variance captured by the first 10 singular directions, enabling compression or visualization.

Quick code / pseudocode

import numpy as np
U,S,Vt=np.linalg.svd(X_centered,full_matrices=False)
X_rank10=U[:,:10]@np.diag(S[:10])@Vt[:10]

Common mistakes

  • Assuming every matrix has a full set of real eigenvectors.
  • Confusing eigenvalues with singular values.
  • Using PCA without centering or considering scale.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does SVD work for rectangular matrices?
  • How does SVD relate to PCA?
  • What does a small singular value mean?
  • What is condition number?

Production / system-design connection

Low-rank methods reduce storage/compute and diagnose redundant representations, but truncation can remove rare yet important directions—validate downstream impact.

5.3

Derivatives, Gradients & Chain Rule

very highsummary
Roles: all, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A derivative measures local change; a gradient collects partial derivatives and points toward steepest increase. Backpropagation efficiently applies the chain rule through a computation graph.

What you must know

  • Partial derivatives
  • Gradient direction
  • Chain rule
  • Jacobian intuition

Why this matters

Gradients connect loss functions to parameter updates. Backpropagation is just efficient chain-rule application over a computation graph.

Intuition

A derivative tells how much an output changes when one input changes slightly. A gradient collects that sensitivity for every input dimension. The chain rule propagates sensitivity through composed operations.

Deep explanation

For a scalar loss L(θ), the gradient ∇θL points in the direction of steepest local increase. Gradient descent moves in the negative direction. The chain rule multiplies local derivatives along computational paths, and reverse-mode autodiff reuses intermediate values efficiently when a scalar loss depends on many parameters.

Math / formal view

If y=f(g(x)), dy/dx = f'(g(x)) g'(x) Gradient: ∇f=[∂f/∂x₁,...,∂f/∂x_d] Update: θ ← θ - η∇θL

Worked example

For L=(wx-y)², dL/dw = 2(wx-y)x. If the prediction is too high and x is positive, the gradient is positive, so gradient descent reduces w.

Quick code / pseudocode

import torch
w=torch.tensor(2.0,requires_grad=True)
x=torch.tensor(3.0); y=torch.tensor(5.0)
loss=(w*x-y)**2
loss.backward()
print(w.grad)

Common mistakes

  • Saying the gradient always points toward the minimum; it points toward local increase.
  • Confusing derivative computation with the optimizer update.
  • Ignoring non-differentiable points or numerical issues.

5.4

Gradient Descent & Learning Rate

very highsummary
Roles: all, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Gradient descent updates parameters in the negative-gradient direction. Too large a learning rate can overshoot or diverge; too small a rate makes optimization painfully slow.

What you must know

  • Batch/SGD/mini-batch
  • Learning rate
  • Momentum
  • Schedulers

Why this matters

Learning rate and optimization behavior are among the most common practical ML/DL interview topics because they directly determine whether training converges.

Intuition

Gradient descent repeatedly asks: which local direction increases the loss fastest? Then it takes a step in the opposite direction. The learning rate controls how large that step is.

Deep explanation

Batch gradient descent uses all samples per update; stochastic/mini-batch methods use noisy gradient estimates that are cheaper and can help exploration. A learning rate that is too high can oscillate or diverge; too low wastes compute and can stall. Schedules, warmup, momentum and adaptive optimizers modify the effective step over time. Non-convex deep networks do not guarantee reaching a global minimum.

Math / formal view

θ_{t+1}=θ_t - η_t g_t, where g_t estimates ∇L(θ_t)

Worked example

If training loss jumps wildly and becomes NaN after a few steps, first lower the learning rate and inspect gradient norms before changing the architecture.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

See how learning rate changes convergence on a simple quadratic.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def optimize(lr,steps=30):
    x=8.0; hist=[]
    for _ in range(steps):
        grad=2*(x-3)          # d/dx (x-3)^2
        x-=lr*grad; hist.append(x)
    return x,hist
for lr in [0.05,0.4,1.1]:
    print(lr,optimize(lr)[0])
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import torch
x=torch.tensor(8.0,requires_grad=True)
opt=torch.optim.SGD([x],lr=.1)
for _ in range(30):
    opt.zero_grad(); loss=(x-3)**2; loss.backward(); opt.step()
print(x.item())
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Training pipelines should log learning rate, loss and gradient/parameter health with checkpoints so failed runs are diagnosable and resumable.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(optimize(.1,60)[0]-3)<1e-4

Common mistakes

  • Assuming a smaller learning rate is always safer or better.
  • Changing many hyperparameters before checking the learning-rate curve.
  • Forgetting optimizer.zero_grad() in PyTorch training loops.

Likely follow-ups

  • What happens if learning rate is too high?
  • Why use mini-batches?
  • What does momentum do?
  • Why use learning-rate warmup?

Production / system-design connection

Training pipelines should log learning rate, loss and gradient/parameter health with checkpoints so failed runs are diagnosable and resumable.

Norms measure vector magnitude; distance functions measure separation; similarity functions such as cosine compare direction. 6.1

Conditional Probability & Bayes Rule

very highsummary
Roles: ds, mle, aie, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Conditional probability updates the probability of an event given evidence. Bayes rule reverses a conditional using prior probability and likelihood, and underlies probabilistic inference and many classifiers.

What you must know

  • P(A|B)
  • Prior/likelihood/posterior
  • Base rates
  • Independence

Why this matters

Conditional probability is the language of updating beliefs from evidence. It appears in Bayesian reasoning, diagnostic tests, anomaly detection, Naive Bayes, calibration, and any interview question where base rates matter.

Intuition

Think of probability as shrinking the universe of possible outcomes after observing evidence. P(A|B) asks: among the cases where B happened, how often did A happen? Bayes rule lets you reverse the direction when P(B|A) is easier to reason about than P(A|B).

Deep explanation

Bayes rule combines a prior belief P(A) with the likelihood of evidence P(B|A), then normalizes by P(B). The base-rate term matters: even a highly accurate detector can have poor positive predictive value when the event is extremely rare. Independence means P(A,B)=P(A)P(B); conditional independence can hold even when marginal independence does not, which is why graphical models and Naive Bayes can be useful simplifications.

Math / formal view

P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) Bayes: P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B) Total probability: P(B)=Σ_i P(B|A_i)P(A_i)

Worked example

Suppose a defect occurs in 1% of parts. A detector catches 95% of defects and falsely flags 5% of good parts. Among flagged parts, the probability of a true defect is far below 95% because the 99% non-defect base rate dominates. This is the classic base-rate lesson.

Quick code / pseudocode

# Bayes update for a binary diagnostic test
prior = 0.01
sensitivity = 0.95
false_positive = 0.05
posterior = sensitivity*prior / (sensitivity*prior + false_positive*(1-prior))
print(round(posterior, 3))

Common mistakes

  • Ignoring the base rate and equating sensitivity with P(defect | positive).
  • Confusing independence with mutual exclusivity.
  • Treating conditional probabilities as symmetric: P(A|B) is not generally P(B|A).

Likely follow-ups

  • What is the difference between independence and conditional independence?
  • Why can a good classifier have low precision on rare events?
  • How does Naive Bayes use conditional independence?
  • What is a prior and when should it matter?

Production / system-design connection

For rare-event systems such as fraud, failures, or safety alerts, calibration and base rates directly determine alert quality. Thresholds should be chosen using posterior risk and operational costs, not accuracy alone.

6.2

Common Probability Distributions

highsummary
Roles: ds, mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Know when Bernoulli, Binomial, Poisson, Normal and related distributions are appropriate. The distribution is a model for the data-generating process, not merely a curve-fitting choice.

What you must know

  • Support
  • Parameters
  • Expectation/variance
  • When each model makes sense

Why this matters

Interviewers use distributions to test whether you can connect a mathematical model to how data is generated instead of selecting a curve by habit.

Intuition

A distribution describes the values a random variable can take and how probability is allocated across them. Choose the family from the mechanism: binary event → Bernoulli, number of successes in fixed trials → Binomial, event counts in an interval → Poisson, continuous additive noise → often approximately Normal.

Deep explanation

Bernoulli models one binary trial; Binomial sums independent Bernoulli trials with constant success probability; Poisson models counts under a constant event-rate approximation; Normal is continuous and symmetric and often appears through aggregation; Exponential models waiting time between Poisson-process events. Real data may violate independence, constant rate, or symmetry assumptions, so goodness-of-fit and domain reasoning matter.

Math / formal view

Bernoulli: P(X=x)=p^x(1-p)^(1-x) Binomial: P(X=k)=C(n,k)p^k(1-p)^(n-k) Poisson: P(X=k)=e^{-λ} λ^k/k! Normal: X ~ N(μ,σ²)

Worked example

Number of support tickets per hour might be modeled as Poisson only if arrivals are roughly independent with a stable rate. If ticket volume has strong time-of-day effects or bursts, a single Poisson model is a poor description.

Quick code / pseudocode

import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(0)
print(rng.binomial(n=20,p=.1,size=5))
print(rng.poisson(lam=3,size=5))

Common mistakes

  • Assuming every continuous variable should be Normal.
  • Using a distribution without checking its support or assumptions.
  • Confusing probability density with probability for continuous variables.

Likely follow-ups

  • When is Poisson a reasonable model?
  • What is the relationship between Bernoulli and Binomial?
  • Why does the Normal distribution appear so often?
  • What distribution would you use for waiting times?

Production / system-design connection

Distribution assumptions influence uncertainty estimates, anomaly thresholds, simulation, forecasting, and likelihood-based losses. Monitor whether the production distribution still resembles the one used during modeling.

6.3

Expectation, Variance & Covariance

very highsummary
Roles: ds, mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Expectation is the long-run average of a random variable; variance measures spread around the mean; covariance measures how two variables vary together, with correlation providing a normalized version.

What you must know

  • Linearity of expectation
  • Variance units
  • Covariance sign
  • Correlation ≠ causation

Why this matters

Expectation, variance and covariance are foundational for losses, estimators, uncertainty, PCA, portfolio/risk reasoning, and the bias–variance trade-off.

Intuition

Expectation is the balance point or long-run average. Variance measures how far values typically spread around that center. Covariance asks whether two variables tend to move together; correlation rescales covariance to a unitless -1 to 1 range.

Deep explanation

Linearity of expectation holds even without independence. Variance is measured in squared units, while standard deviation returns to the original units. Covariance depends on scale; correlation normalizes by both standard deviations. Zero covariance means no linear relationship but does not imply independence except under special distributional assumptions.

Math / formal view

E[aX+bY]=aE[X]+bE[Y] Var(X)=E[(X-E[X])²]=E[X²]-E[X]² Cov(X,Y)=E[(X-E[X])(Y-E[Y])] Corr(X,Y)=Cov(X,Y)/(σ_X σ_Y)

Worked example

If model error has mean near zero but very high variance, predictions are unbiased on average yet individually unreliable. Reporting only the mean error would hide this instability.

Quick code / pseudocode

import numpy as np
x=np.array([1,2,3,4])
y=np.array([2,4,5,8])
print(x.mean(), x.var(ddof=1))
print(np.cov(x,y,ddof=1)[0,1])
print(np.corrcoef(x,y)[0,1])

Common mistakes

  • Saying correlation implies causation.
  • Forgetting that variance is in squared units.
  • Assuming zero correlation means independence.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why is covariance scale-dependent?
  • What is the difference between population and sample variance?
  • How does covariance connect to PCA?
  • When does zero covariance imply independence?

Production / system-design connection

Use variance and covariance to understand feature redundancy, uncertainty, drift, and instability across cohorts. Correlations can change after deployment, so they should be monitored rather than treated as permanent properties.

6.4

Law of Large Numbers & Central Limit Theorem

highsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

The law of large numbers explains why sample averages stabilize around expectations. The CLT explains why normalized sums often approach a Normal distribution, enabling many confidence intervals and tests.

What you must know

  • Different theorems
  • Sampling distribution
  • Conditions matter
  • Why Normal approximations appear

Why this matters

The LLN and CLT explain why averages stabilize and why Normal-based confidence intervals and tests often work even when individual observations are not Normal.

Intuition

The law of large numbers is about where the sample average goes as sample size increases. The central limit theorem is about the shape of the sampling distribution after centering and scaling. They answer different questions.

Deep explanation

Under suitable conditions, the sample mean converges to the population expectation (LLN). Separately, the standardized sum or mean converges in distribution toward a Normal law (CLT). The approximation can be poor for small samples, heavy tails, strong dependence, or non-identically distributed data; blindly invoking the CLT is not a substitute for checking the data-generating process.

Math / formal view

LLN: X̄_n → μ as n→∞ (in an appropriate convergence sense) CLT: √n (X̄_n-μ)/σ ⇒ N(0,1)

Worked example

Individual transaction amounts may be strongly right-skewed, but the distribution of the average transaction amount across many independent samples can become approximately Normal as sample size grows.

Quick code / pseudocode

import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(0)
means=[rng.exponential(1,size=100).mean() for _ in range(5000)]
print(np.mean(means), np.std(means))

Common mistakes

  • Saying the CLT means the raw data becomes Normal.
  • Treating LLN and CLT as the same theorem.
  • Ignoring dependence or heavy-tailed behavior.

Likely follow-ups

  • Does the CLT require the original data to be Normal?
  • What changes when observations are dependent?
  • Why does standard error shrink like 1/sqrt(n)?
  • What is the difference between convergence in probability and in distribution?

Production / system-design connection

Many dashboards and experiments use Normal approximations for uncertainty. For small or highly skewed samples, bootstrap or exact methods may be safer.

6.7

Monte Carlo Simulation

highsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Monte Carlo approximates expectations or probabilities with repeated random samples. Error typically shrinks with the square root of sample count, so simulation is flexible but can be computationally expensive.

What you must know

  • Use simulation when analytic calculation is hard.
  • Random seeds improve reproducibility, not statistical validity.
  • Variance reduction can improve efficiency.

Why this matters

Monte Carlo Simulation is a recurring foundation across data science and machine learning because it affects both theoretical correctness and practical system behavior.

Intuition

Use simulation when analytic calculation is hard.

Deep explanation

Monte Carlo approximates expectations or probabilities with repeated random samples. Error typically shrinks with the square root of sample count, so simulation is flexible but can be computationally expensive. Random seeds improve reproducibility, not statistical validity. Variance reduction can improve efficiency. The interview-level skill is not merely recalling the definition: explain the assumptions, what diagnostic evidence you would inspect, and what alternative you would choose when those assumptions fail.

Worked example

Estimate probability a capacity system overloads by simulating uncertain daily demand.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Estimate a probability with Monte Carlo simulation.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(0)
n=200_000
x=rng.random((n,2))
inside=(x[:,0]**2+x[:,1]**2)<=1
pi_hat=4*inside.mean()
print(pi_hat)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
batches=inside.reshape(200,-1).mean(axis=1)*4
print('SE',batches.std(ddof=1)/np.sqrt(len(batches)))
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Use deterministic seeds for tests, but in production report Monte Carlo error and ensure simulated distributions reflect the decision problem.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(pi_hat-np.pi)<0.03

Common mistakes

  • Using the concept mechanically without checking assumptions or data semantics.
  • Reporting one metric/result without examining uncertainty, slices or failure modes.

Likely follow-ups

  • What assumptions or limitations does Monte Carlo Simulation have?

mediumsummary
Roles: ds, as

Condition on useful groups, solve within each group, then average using group probabilities. These identities are powerful for mixture distributions, debugging aggregate metrics and Bayesian reasoning.

What you must know

  • P(A)=sum P(A|B)P(B).
  • E[X]=E[E[X|Y]].
  • Stratification can explain aggregate differences.

Why this matters

Law of Total Probability & Total Expectation is a recurring foundation across data science and machine learning because it affects both theoretical correctness and practical system behavior.

Intuition

P(A)=sum P(A|B)P(B).

Deep explanation

Condition on useful groups, solve within each group, then average using group probabilities. These identities are powerful for mixture distributions, debugging aggregate metrics and Bayesian reasoning. E[X]=E[E[X|Y]]. Stratification can explain aggregate differences. The interview-level skill is not merely recalling the definition: explain the assumptions, what diagnostic evidence you would inspect, and what alternative you would choose when those assumptions fail.

Worked example

Overall conversion is a weighted average of device-specific conversion rates.

7.1

Confidence Intervals

very highsummary
Roles: ds, da, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A frequentist 95% confidence interval is produced by a procedure that would contain the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples. It is not literally a 95% probability statement about a fixed parameter after observing the data.

What you must know

  • Standard error
  • Coverage interpretation
  • Sample size
  • Assumptions

Why this matters

Confidence intervals test whether you understand uncertainty rather than reporting point estimates as if they were exact.

Intuition

A point estimate gives one number; a confidence interval shows the range of values compatible with sampling uncertainty under a specified procedure. Wider intervals mean more uncertainty.

Deep explanation

In frequentist inference, the parameter is fixed and the interval is random before sampling. A 95% confidence procedure has 95% long-run coverage under its assumptions. Width depends on standard error, confidence level and sample size. Correct coverage can fail when assumptions, dependence, or repeated peeking are ignored.

Math / formal view

Generic form: estimate ± critical_value × standard_error For a mean with large n: X̄ ± z_(1-α/2) σ/√n

Worked example

If a conversion lift is estimated at +1.2 percentage points with a 95% CI of [-0.2, 2.6], the data are compatible with both a small negative and a useful positive effect; the point estimate alone is not enough.

Quick code / pseudocode

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
x=np.array([10,11,12,9,13,12,11])
mean=x.mean(); se=stats.sem(x)
print(stats.t.interval(.95, df=len(x)-1, loc=mean, scale=se))

Common mistakes

  • Saying there is a 95% probability the fixed frequentist parameter lies in this observed interval.
  • Reporting a CI without the assumptions or sample design.
  • Treating a narrow but biased interval as trustworthy.

Likely follow-ups

  • How does sample size affect interval width?
  • What is the difference between a confidence interval and prediction interval?
  • When would you use a bootstrap interval?
  • How does repeated testing affect coverage?

Production / system-design connection

Confidence intervals are useful for experiment effects, model metrics, latency estimates and business KPIs. Slice-level intervals can reveal when apparent subgroup differences are mostly sampling noise.

7.2

Hypothesis Testing & p-values

very highsummary
Roles: ds, da, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis and test assumptions are true, of seeing a result at least as extreme as the observed one. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

What you must know

  • Null/alternative
  • Test statistic
  • Type I/II errors
  • Statistical vs practical significance

Why this matters

Data Scientist interviews often test whether you can reason about experiments instead of mechanically running scipy.stats functions.

Intuition

Start by assuming there is no real effect (the null). Ask how surprising your observed result would be under that assumption. A small p-value means the observation would be unusual under the null—it does not directly tell you the probability that the null is false.

Deep explanation

A hypothesis test requires a null/alternative, a test statistic, assumptions and a decision threshold. Type I error is a false positive; Type II is a false negative. Statistical significance is not necessarily business significance, which is why effect size and confidence intervals matter.

Math / formal view

p-value = P(test statistic at least as extreme as observed | H₀ and assumptions)

Worked example

A tiny conversion lift can be statistically significant with millions of users but economically irrelevant. Always report effect size and uncertainty.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Compute a simple two-sample mean test and connect the statistic to the null hypothesis.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import math
a=[10,11,9,12,10,11]; b=[13,12,14,11,13,14]
def mean(x): return sum(x)/len(x)
def var(x):
    m=mean(x); return sum((v-m)**2 for v in x)/(len(x)-1)
se=math.sqrt(var(a)/len(a)+var(b)/len(b))
t=(mean(b)-mean(a))/se
print('difference',mean(b)-mean(a),'t statistic',t)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from scipy.stats import ttest_ind
print(ttest_ind(b,a,equal_var=False))
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

In product experimentation, predefine the primary metric, sample-size/power plan, stopping rule and guardrail metrics before observing the result.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert mean(b)>mean(a)
assert t>1

Common mistakes

  • “p=0.03 means there is a 97% chance the alternative is true.” — incorrect.
  • Treating p<0.05 as automatically important.
  • Choosing the test after repeatedly looking at results.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is statistical power?
  • Type I vs Type II error?
  • When would you use a non-parametric test?
  • How does multiple testing change interpretation?

7.3

MLE vs MAP

highsummary
Roles: ds, mle, da, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Maximum likelihood chooses parameters that make observed data most likely. MAP adds a prior and chooses the most probable parameters after combining prior and likelihood; many regularizers can be interpreted as MAP priors.

What you must know

  • Likelihood vs probability
  • Prior
  • Regularization link
  • Bayesian interpretation

Why this matters

MLE and MAP connect probability, optimization and regularization. They help explain why familiar losses such as cross-entropy and squared error arise from probabilistic assumptions.

Intuition

MLE asks which parameters make the observed data most plausible. MAP asks the same question but also incorporates what parameter values were plausible before seeing the data.

Deep explanation

Given independent observations, MLE maximizes the likelihood or equivalently the log-likelihood. MAP maximizes log likelihood plus log prior. A Gaussian prior over weights produces an L2-style penalty; a Laplace prior produces an L1-style penalty. MLE and MAP return point estimates, unlike full Bayesian inference which maintains a posterior distribution.

Math / formal view

MLE: θ̂ = argmax_θ p(D|θ) MAP: θ̂ = argmax_θ p(D|θ)p(θ) = argmax [log p(D|θ)+log p(θ)]

Worked example

Linear regression with Gaussian observation noise leads to minimizing squared error. Adding a zero-mean Gaussian prior on coefficients produces an L2-regularized objective, giving a MAP interpretation of ridge regression.

Quick code / pseudocode

# Negative log-likelihood + L2 prior (schematic)
loss = data_negative_log_likelihood + lambda_ * (weights**2).sum()

Common mistakes

  • Calling the likelihood a probability distribution over parameters.
  • Saying MAP is full Bayesian inference.
  • Assuming regularization always corresponds to the same prior regardless of formulation.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why do we maximize log-likelihood instead of likelihood?
  • How does ridge regression connect to a Gaussian prior?
  • What is the difference between MAP and posterior mean?
  • When does the prior matter less?

Production / system-design connection

Probabilistic objectives make uncertainty assumptions explicit. If noise characteristics or class probabilities shift, likelihood-based training assumptions and calibration can become wrong.

Sampling Distributions & Standard Error

very highsummary
Roles: ds, da, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A sampling distribution describes how an estimator would vary across repeated samples. Standard error measures that estimator uncertainty; it is not the standard deviation of the raw observations.

What you must know

  • Estimator variability shrinks with more information/sample size.
  • SE and population SD answer different questions.
  • Sampling design affects uncertainty.

Why this matters

Sampling Distributions & Standard Error appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Estimator variability shrinks with more information/sample size.

Deep explanation

A sampling distribution describes how an estimator would vary across repeated samples. Standard error measures that estimator uncertainty; it is not the standard deviation of the raw observations. SE and population SD answer different questions. Sampling design affects uncertainty. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

The mean order value may have SD €40 across orders but a much smaller SE for the estimated population mean.

Common mistakes

7.5

Bootstrap & Resampling

highsummary
Roles: ds, da, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

The bootstrap approximates an estimator’s sampling distribution by repeatedly resampling the observed dataset with replacement. It is useful when analytic standard errors are difficult but the sample is reasonably representative.

What you must know

  • Resample rows with replacement.
  • Recompute the statistic each time.
  • Use the empirical distribution for uncertainty.

Why this matters

Bootstrap & Resampling appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Resample rows with replacement.

Deep explanation

The bootstrap approximates an estimator’s sampling distribution by repeatedly resampling the observed dataset with replacement. It is useful when analytic standard errors are difficult but the sample is reasonably representative. Recompute the statistic each time. Use the empirical distribution for uncertainty. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Bootstrap the difference in median delivery times between two methods to form an interval.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Estimate uncertainty with a nonparametric bootstrap.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(0)
x=np.array([2.,3.,4.,5.,8.,9.])
stats=np.array([rng.choice(x,len(x),replace=True).mean() for _ in range(5000)])
ci=np.quantile(stats,[.025,.975])
print(ci)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from scipy.stats import bootstrap
res=bootstrap((x,),np.mean,random_state=0)
print(res.confidence_interval)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Package bootstrap configuration with the estimator definition and random seed; use it when analytic uncertainty is unavailable and monitor whether the production sample remains representative.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert ci[0] < x.mean() < ci[1]

Common mistakes

  • Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
  • Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.

  • Pre-register primary metrics when possible.

Why this matters

More tests → more opportunities for false positives.

Deep explanation

Family-wise methods such as Bonferroni control any false positive; FDR methods such as Benjamini–Hochberg control the expected proportion among discoveries. FWER and FDR are different guarantees. Pre-register primary metrics when possible. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Testing 100 product metrics at 5% individually will produce apparent wins by chance even if nothing changed.

A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

A strong answer connects the formal idea to validation, data requirements and failure modes instead of treating the method as a recipe.

Bayesian Updating: Prior, Likelihood & Posterior

highsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Bayesian inference updates prior beliefs with evidence through the likelihood to produce a posterior distribution. The posterior represents uncertainty about parameters after observing data.

What you must know

  • Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior.
  • Priors can regularize sparse/noisy problems.
  • Posterior predictive checks validate consequences of the model.

Bayesian Updating: Prior, Likelihood & Posterior appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior.

Deep explanation

Bayesian inference updates prior beliefs with evidence through the likelihood to produce a posterior distribution. The posterior represents uncertainty about parameters after observing data. Priors can regularize sparse/noisy problems. Posterior predictive checks validate consequences of the model. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

mediumsummary

8.3

Credible Intervals vs Confidence Intervals

highsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A Bayesian credible interval is a probability statement about a parameter under the posterior; a frequentist confidence interval is a procedure that covers the fixed parameter at a stated long-run frequency.

What you must know

  • Interpretations differ even when numerical intervals look similar.
  • Bayesian intervals depend on prior/model.
  • Frequentist coverage is about repeated procedures.

Why this matters

Credible Intervals vs Confidence Intervals appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Interpretations differ even when numerical intervals look similar.

Deep explanation

A Bayesian credible interval is a probability statement about a parameter under the posterior; a frequentist confidence interval is a procedure that covers the fixed parameter at a stated long-run frequency. Bayesian intervals depend on prior/model. Frequentist coverage is about repeated procedures. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

A 95% credible interval can be described as containing 95% posterior probability for the parameter under the model.

Missingness: MCAR, MAR & MNAR

highsummary
Roles: ds, da
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Missing values can be completely random, explainable by observed variables, or related to the missing value itself. The mechanism matters because naive imputation can bias estimates and hide useful missingness signals.

What you must know

  • MCAR: missing independent of data.
  • MAR: missingness depends on observed variables.
  • MNAR: missingness depends on unobserved/missing value.

Missingness: MCAR, MAR & MNAR appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

MCAR: missing independent of data.

Deep explanation

Missing values can be completely random, explainable by observed variables, or related to the missing value itself. The mechanism matters because naive imputation can bias estimates and hide useful missingness signals. MAR: missingness depends on observed variables. MNAR: missingness depends on unobserved/missing value. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Income nonresponse may be related to income itself, making simple mean imputation particularly questionable.

45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Linear regression models the target as a weighted sum of features and typically minimizes squared error. Know its assumptions, how coefficients are interpreted, and why multicollinearity/outliers can matter.

What you must know

  • OLS objective
  • Residual assumptions
  • R²
  • Regularized variants

Why this matters

Linear regression is simple enough to derive but rich enough to test assumptions, loss functions, interpretation, regularization and statistical reasoning.

Intuition

The model fits a plane through feature space. Each coefficient changes the predicted target by a constant amount per unit feature change, holding other features fixed.

Deep explanation

Ordinary least squares minimizes squared residuals. Under standard assumptions it has useful unbiasedness/inference properties, but prediction can still work when inference assumptions are imperfect. Multicollinearity makes coefficients unstable; nonlinear relationships require transformed features or other models; heteroscedasticity affects standard errors. Ridge/Lasso trade bias for stability/sparsity.

Math / formal view

ŷ = Xβ + b OLS: minimize ||y-Xβ||₂² Closed form when invertible: β̂=(XᵀX)^{-1}Xᵀy

Worked example

If house price increases roughly linearly with area but location shifts the baseline, include both area and encoded location. A strong coefficient does not by itself prove area causally changes price.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement ordinary least squares with gradient descent, then compare it with scikit-learn.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(0)
X=rng.normal(size=(200,1)); y=3*X[:,0]+2+rng.normal(0,.3,200)
Xb=np.c_[np.ones(len(X)),X]
w=np.zeros(2); lr=.05
for _ in range(1000):
    pred=Xb@w
    grad=(2/len(Xb))*Xb.T@(pred-y)
    w-=lr*grad
print('from scratch:',w)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
m=LinearRegression().fit(X,y)
print('sklearn:',m.intercept_,m.coef_)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Monitor residual distribution, drift, coefficient stability and extrapolation. Linear models can be excellent baselines because they are cheap, interpretable and easy to debug.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(w[0]-2)<0.2
assert abs(w[1]-3)<0.2

Common mistakes

  • Saying linear regression requires every feature to be Normally distributed.
  • Interpreting coefficients causally without design assumptions.
  • Ignoring multicollinearity and residual structure.

10.2

Logistic Regression

very highsummary
Roles: ds, mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Logistic regression models log-odds as a linear function of features and maps them through a sigmoid to a probability. Training usually minimizes log loss rather than MSE.

What you must know

  • Sigmoid
  • Log odds
  • Decision threshold
  • Regularization

Why this matters

It is one of the best interview algorithms because it combines linear models, probability, classification, loss functions and interpretability.

Intuition

The model computes a linear score and passes it through a sigmoid so the output lies between 0 and 1. A threshold then converts probability into a class.

Deep explanation

Logistic regression models log-odds linearly. It is typically trained with binary cross-entropy / negative log likelihood. Coefficients describe additive changes in log-odds per unit feature change, conditional on the other features.

Math / formal view

p(y=1|x)=σ(wᵀx+b), σ(z)=1/(1+e⁻ᶻ) log(p/(1-p)) = wᵀx+b

Worked example

In rare-failure prediction, fit probabilities, evaluate PR metrics and choose a threshold from the false-negative/false-positive cost rather than default 0.5.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Build binary logistic regression and verify probabilities/decision boundary.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(1)
X=rng.normal(size=(300,2)); y=(X[:,0]+.7*X[:,1]>0).astype(float)
Xb=np.c_[np.ones(len(X)),X]; w=np.zeros(3)
def sigmoid(z): return 1/(1+np.exp(-z))
for _ in range(2000):
    p=sigmoid(Xb@w)
    w-=0.1*(Xb.T@(p-y)/len(y))
print('accuracy',((sigmoid(Xb@w)>=.5)==y).mean())
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
m=LogisticRegression().fit(X,y)
print(m.score(X,y),m.predict_proba(X[:3]))
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

It is often a superb baseline because it trains fast, is easy to calibrate/interpret and exposes whether more complex models are truly necessary.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
p=sigmoid(Xb@w)
assert np.all((0<=p)&(p<=1))
assert ((p>=.5)==y).mean()>.9

Common mistakes

  • Calling it a regression model because of the name without explaining classification.
  • Assuming 0.5 is always the right threshold.
  • Interpreting coefficients causally.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why use log loss instead of MSE?
  • What does regularization do?
  • How do you handle nonlinearity?
  • How do coefficients map to odds ratios?

Production / system-design connection

It is often a superb baseline because it trains fast, is easy to calibrate/interpret and exposes whether more complex models are truly necessary.

10.3

Linear Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics

very highsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

For inference, linear regression relies on assumptions about functional form, independent errors, variance structure and error distribution; for prediction, diagnostics still reveal misspecification, outliers and extrapolation risk.

What you must know

  • Inspect residual vs fitted plots.
  • Check leverage/influence, not just residual size.
  • Heteroscedasticity affects uncertainty estimates.

Why this matters

Linear Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Inspect residual vs fitted plots.

Deep explanation

For inference, linear regression relies on assumptions about functional form, independent errors, variance structure and error distribution; for prediction, diagnostics still reveal misspecification, outliers and extrapolation risk. Check leverage/influence, not just residual size. Heteroscedasticity affects uncertainty estimates. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Residual variance increasing with fitted revenue suggests transformation, weighted/robust methods or different uncertainty estimates.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
  • Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.

Likely follow-ups

  • Tune strength with validation.

Intuition

Regularization trades variance for bias.

Deep explanation

Ridge uses L2 regularization to shrink coefficients; Lasso uses L1 and can set coefficients exactly to zero; Elastic Net combines both, often helping with correlated features. Scale features before coefficient-penalty comparisons. Tune strength with validation. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

For thousands of correlated marketing features, Elastic Net can stabilize estimates while selecting a sparse-ish subset.

11.1

Decision Trees

very highsummary
Roles: ds, mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Decision trees recursively split the feature space to make child nodes purer. They capture nonlinear interactions and require little preprocessing, but deep trees overfit easily.

What you must know

  • Gini/entropy
  • Split criterion
  • Depth
  • Feature importance caveats

Why this matters

Decision trees introduce recursive partitioning, impurity measures, overfitting and the foundation for random forests and gradient boosting.

Intuition

A tree repeatedly asks simple questions that split the data into purer groups. Each path from root to leaf is an interpretable set of rules.

Deep explanation

For classification, splits often maximize impurity reduction using Gini or entropy; regression trees reduce squared/absolute error. Trees naturally model nonlinear interactions and mixed scales but are high variance: a small data change can alter structure. Depth, minimum samples and pruning regularize them. Greedy split selection is local, not globally optimal.

Math / formal view

Gini = 1-Σ_k p_k² Entropy = -Σ_k p_k log p_k Split gain = parent impurity - weighted child impurities

Worked example

A failure classifier might first split on load, then material type, then temperature. The interactions are learned without manually creating load×material features.

Quick code / pseudocode

from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
m=DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5,min_samples_leaf=20,random_state=0)
m.fit(X_train,y_train)

Common mistakes

  • Assuming deeper trees are always better.
  • Treating feature-importance scores as causal.
  • Ignoring class imbalance or leakage because trees handle preprocessing well.

Likely follow-ups

  • Gini vs entropy?
  • Why do trees overfit?
  • How does pruning help?
  • Why do ensembles improve trees?

Production / system-design connection

Tree models are strong tabular baselines. Validate input ranges/categories and monitor feature distributions because splits can behave unexpectedly outside training support.

11.2

Random Forest

highsummary
Roles: ds, mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Random forests reduce tree variance by training many trees on bootstrapped samples and random feature subsets, then averaging or voting their predictions.

What you must know

  • Bagging
  • Feature randomness
  • OOB intuition
  • Bias/variance

Why this matters

Random forests are robust tabular baselines and illustrate how bagging reduces variance.

Intuition

Train many decision trees on different bootstrap samples and random feature subsets, then average/vote. Individual trees are unstable; averaging makes the ensemble more stable.

Deep explanation

Bootstrap sampling decorrelates training data, and random feature selection decorrelates trees further. Averaging reduces variance when errors are not perfectly correlated. Out-of-bag samples can estimate performance. Forests capture nonlinear interactions with modest preprocessing but can be large/slow and less interpretable than a single tree.

Math / formal view

Regression forest: ŷ(x)=1/T Σ_t h_t(x); classification averages probabilities/votes.

Worked example

On mixed tabular sensor/product data, a forest can establish a strong nonlinear baseline before investing in neural networks.

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Xtr,Xte,ytr,yte=train_test_split(X,y,test_size=.25,random_state=0,stratify=y)

p=m.predict_proba(Xte)[:,1]
auc=roc_auc_score(yte,p)
print(auc)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Version features and forest hyperparameters; monitor score calibration and feature/data drift rather than relying only on training feature importance.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
