16.7

Trend, Seasonality, Cycles & Remainder

very highsummary
Roles: ds, da, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A time series can contain trend, seasonal patterns, longer cycles and irregular remainder. I identify these structures before selecting a model because validation and feature construction depend on them.

What you must know

  • Plot the series first.
  • Seasonality has a known calendar frequency; cycles need not.
  • Multiple seasonalities can coexist.

Why this matters

Trend, Seasonality, Cycles & Remainder appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Plot the series first.

Deep explanation

A time series can contain trend, seasonal patterns, longer cycles and irregular remainder. I identify these structures before selecting a model because validation and feature construction depend on them. Seasonality has a known calendar frequency; cycles need not. Multiple seasonalities can coexist. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Hourly demand may have daily and weekly seasonality plus a long-term growth trend.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
  • Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.

Likely follow-ups

  • What assumptions does Trend, Seasonality, Cycles & Remainder make?
  • How would you validate or debug Trend, Seasonality, Cycles & Remainder in practice?

16.8

Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage

very highsummary
Roles: ds, da, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Lag and rolling features summarize past information, but they must be constructed using only data available at prediction time. Centered windows or post-outcome aggregates silently leak the future.

What you must know

  • Shift before rolling when necessary.
  • Feature availability timestamp matters.
  • Use the same pipeline in backtests and production.

Why this matters

Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Shift before rolling when necessary.

Deep explanation

Lag and rolling features summarize past information, but they must be constructed using only data available at prediction time. Centered windows or post-outcome aggregates silently leak the future. Feature availability timestamp matters. Use the same pipeline in backtests and production. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Predict tomorrow’s demand using demand up to today, never a 7-day centered moving average that includes tomorrow.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
  • Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.

Likely follow-ups

  • What assumptions does Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage make?
  • How would you validate or debug Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage in practice?

Production / system-design connection

In production, validate assumptions on real data, monitor the quantities that can drift, and keep a simple baseline so added complexity has a measurable reason to exist.

16.9

Naive, Seasonal-Naive & Drift Baselines

very highsummary
Roles: ds, da, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Hazard and survival encode related but different views. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

18.2

Kaplan–Meier Estimator & Log-rank Test

highsummary
Roles: ds, da
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Kaplan–Meier estimates the survival curve nonparametrically by multiplying conditional survival probabilities at event times. The log-rank test compares survival curves across groups under assumptions.

What you must know

  • Handles right censoring.
  • Median survival comes from S(t)=0.5 when reached.
  • Curves can cross, complicating simple comparisons.

Why this matters

Kaplan–Meier Estimator & Log-rank Test appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Handles right censoring.

Deep explanation

Kaplan–Meier estimates the survival curve nonparametrically by multiplying conditional survival probabilities at event times. The log-rank test compares survival curves across groups under assumptions. Median survival comes from S(t)=0.5 when reached. Curves can cross, complicating simple comparisons. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Compare retention survival for two acquisition channels while accounting for recent users who have not yet churned.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Fit and inspect a Kaplan–Meier survival curve.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
t=np.array([1,2,2,3,5],float); e=np.array([1,1,0,1,0])
s=1.0
for time in sorted(set(t[e==1])):
    at_risk=(t>=time).sum(); events=((t==time)&(e==1)).sum(); s*=1-events/at_risk
    print(time,s)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from lifelines import KaplanMeierFitter
km=KaplanMeierFitter().fit(t,event_observed=e)
print(km.survival_function_)

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert 0 <= s <= 1

19.1

Convexity & Optimization Intuition

highsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A convex objective has no bad local minima: any local minimum is global. Deep networks are non-convex, so optimization relies on practical gradient methods rather than global-optimum guarantees.

What you must know

  • Convex set/function
  • Local vs global optimum
  • Learning rate
  • Conditioning

Why this matters

Convexity explains why some optimization problems are globally well-behaved while deep-network training is not.

Intuition

A convex bowl has no deceptive local valleys: the line segment between two points stays above the function, and any local minimum is global.

Deep explanation

For differentiable convex f, f(y)≥f(x)+∇f(x)ᵀ(y-x). Strong convexity gives curvature bounds and faster guarantees. Linear/logistic regression with suitable losses can be convex in parameters, while neural networks are highly non-convex. Non-convex does not mean impossible; gradient methods can still find useful solutions in overparameterized landscapes.

Math / formal view

Convex: f(θx+(1-θ)y) ≤ θf(x)+(1-θ)f(y), θ∈[0,1]

Worked example

Least-squares linear regression has a convex quadratic objective; changing initialization does not create distinct bad local minima in the same way a deep network can.

Common mistakes

  • Saying convex functions are always easy regardless of conditioning/scale.
  • Calling every smooth loss convex.
  • Assuming non-convex training necessarily gets stuck in poor local minima.

Likely follow-ups

  • Convex vs strongly convex?
  • Why is linear regression convex?
  • Is logistic regression convex?
  • What does condition number affect?

Production / system-design connection

Convex baselines are valuable for reliability and debugging; if a complex model barely beats one, production complexity may not be justified.

20.1

Recall@K & Ranking Evaluation

highsummary
Roles: mle, ds, da
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Recall@K asks whether relevant items appear in the top K recommendations. It fits reviewer/recommender systems better than plain classification accuracy because users receive ranked candidates.

What you must know

  • Top-k ranking
  • Multiple relevant items
  • MRR/NDCG alternatives
  • Candidate set

Why this matters

Ranking systems are judged by whether relevant items appear near the top, so Recall@K is often more meaningful than classification accuracy.

Intuition

For each query, look only at the first K recommendations and ask what fraction of the relevant items were recovered.

Deep explanation

Recall@K ignores ordering within the top K; Precision@K penalizes irrelevant returned items; MRR emphasizes the rank of the first relevant result; nDCG handles graded relevance and position discounts. Metric choice depends on how many relevant items exist and what users actually inspect. Offline labels may be incomplete—unobserved does not always mean irrelevant.

Math / formal view

Recall@K = (# relevant items in top K)/(# relevant items)

Worked example

If the true reviewer set contains 2 people and one appears in the top 10, Recall@10=0.5 for that PR. In a single-label formulation, the metric becomes whether the one known reviewer appears in top K.

Common mistakes

  • Saying Recall@10=77% means 77% of the top 10 suggestions are correct.
  • Ignoring multiple relevant reviewers.
  • Comparing ranking metrics without matching candidate sets/label definitions.

Likely follow-ups

  • Precision@K vs Recall@K?
  • What is MRR?
  • Why nDCG?
  • How do incomplete labels affect offline evaluation?

Production / system-design connection

Track ranking quality by query cohort and candidate availability; online acceptance/merge latency may be better business metrics than offline Recall@K alone.

20.2

Popularity Bias in Recommenders

mediumsummary
Roles: mle, ds, da
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Highly active/popular entities can dominate recommendations even when niche specialists are more relevant. Mitigation can include debiasing, re-ranking, diversity constraints or separating expertise from activity.

What you must know

  • Exposure bias
  • Hub problem
  • Re-ranking
  • Offline/online evaluation

Why this matters

Recommenders often over-recommend popular items/users because historical interactions are heavily skewed, reducing personalization and specialist discovery.

Intuition

If one maintainer reviews almost everything, the model can learn “recommend the maintainer” and score well without learning topic-specific expertise.

Deep explanation

Bias comes from exposure and label imbalance: popular candidates have more training edges and more chances to be selected. Mitigations include candidate normalization, degree-aware features/losses, debiasing embeddings, diversity constraints and separating expertise from activity. Improvements should be validated against relevance, not just forced equal exposure.

Worked example

Centroid subtraction can remove a generic “core team” direction so niche PR text surfaces specialists rather than the same high-degree maintainer every time.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming popularity is always bad—high activity may be a valid reliability signal.
  • Forcing equal recommendation rates regardless of relevance.
  • Evaluating only aggregate Recall@K and missing long-tail quality.

Likely follow-ups

  • How would you measure popularity bias?
  • What is exposure bias?
  • How do you balance expertise and activity?
  • Could debiasing hurt accuracy?

Production / system-design connection

Monitor recommendation concentration, long-tail coverage, acceptance and workload distribution. Provide business controls when activity/availability is operationally important.

import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(0)

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement a tiny BM25 scorer and compare lexical ranking.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import math,re
docs=['red bolt m8 stainless','blue bolt m6 steel','m8 stainless anchor bolt']
q='m8 stainless bolt'.split()
tok=[re.findall(r'\w+',doc.lower()) for doc in docs]
N=len(tok); avg=sum(map(len,tok))/N
def bm25(i,k1=1.5,b=.75):
    s=0.0
    for term in q:
        df=sum(term in x for x in tok)
        idf=math.log(1+(N-df+.5)/(df+.5))
        tf=tok[i].count(term)
        if tf:
            s+=idf*tf*(k1+1)/(tf+k1*(1-b+b*len(tok[i])/avg))
    return s
print([bm25(i) for i in range(N)])
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
v=TfidfVectorizer().fit(docs+[' '.join(q)])
M=v.transform(docs); qq=v.transform([' '.join(q)])
print(cosine_similarity(qq,M)[0])
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Keep lexical retrieval as a production baseline even with vectors; exact identifiers, rare codes and filters often benefit from BM25/hybrid search.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert max(range(N),key=bm25) in {0,2}

22.1

Graph ML Fundamentals

highsummary
Roles: mle, ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A graph represents entities as nodes and relationships as edges. ML on graphs combines node/edge features with graph structure to predict node labels, links, graph properties or rankings.

What you must know

  • Nodes/edges
  • Directed vs undirected
  • Heterogeneous graphs
  • Tasks

Why this matters

Graph ML starts with representing entities and relationships explicitly; interviews expect you to know nodes, edges, direction, heterogeneity and graph-specific leakage.

Intuition

A graph stores objects as nodes and relationships as edges. Features live on nodes/edges, while topology itself provides information that ordinary tabular models may miss.

Deep explanation

Graphs may be directed/undirected, weighted, homogeneous or heterogeneous with multiple node/edge types. Degree, neighborhoods, paths and connected components describe structure. Adjacency matrices/lists encode connectivity. In ML, splits require care: edges/nodes from the future can leak information, and message passing can indirectly expose validation/test structure depending on the setup.

Math / formal view

Adjacency A_ij=1 (or weight) when an edge connects i→j. Degree d_i=Σ_j A_ij for a simple directed-out degree.

Worked example

A developer–PR graph has two node types and “authored”/“reviewed” edges. The same PR text alone misses historical reviewer relationships that graph structure captures.

Common mistakes

  • Treating graph rows as independent samples.
  • Ignoring edge direction/type.
  • Randomly splitting temporal interaction graphs without leakage analysis.

Likely follow-ups

  • Homogeneous vs heterogeneous graph?
  • Directed vs undirected?
  • What is node degree?
  • How do you split graph data?

Production / system-design connection

Graph freshness, edge timestamps and entity resolution matter as much as the GNN. Build reproducible snapshot logic for training and online updates.

22.2

Message Passing in GNNs

highsummary
Roles: mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

GNN layers aggregate information from neighbors and combine it with the current node representation. Repeating layers expands the receptive field over graph hops.

What you must know

  • Aggregate
  • Update
  • Permutation invariance
  • Oversmoothing

Why this matters

Message passing is the core abstraction behind many GNNs and explains how local graph structure becomes learned node representations.

Intuition

Each node receives summaries from neighbors, combines them with its own state, and repeats this for several layers so information travels multiple hops.

Deep explanation

A generic layer computes messages from neighbors, aggregates them with a permutation-invariant function such as sum/mean/max, then updates the node representation. After k layers, a node typically depends on k-hop neighborhoods. Too many layers can lead to over-smoothing or over-squashing; high-degree neighborhoods may require sampling.

Math / formal view

m_v = AGG_{u∈N(v)} M(h_v,h_u,e_uv); h_v' = U(h_v,m_v)

Worked example

In reviewer recommendation, a developer embedding can incorporate the PRs they reviewed; another layer can indirectly incorporate relationships from nearby developers/PRs.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking neighbor order should affect a permutation-invariant graph aggregator.
  • Adding many layers without considering oversmoothing.
  • Ignoring edge features/types when they carry semantics.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is over-smoothing?
  • Why must aggregation be permutation invariant?
  • How many hops does k layers see?
  • What is neighbor sampling?

Production / system-design connection

Bound neighborhood expansion for memory/latency and monitor degree skew; giant hubs can dominate compute and representation quality.

22.3

GraphSAGE

very highsummary
Roles: mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

GraphSAGE learns aggregation functions that combine sampled neighbor features, enabling inductive embeddings for nodes that were not present during training.

What you must know

  • Inductive learning
  • Neighbor sampling
  • Aggregation
  • New nodes

Why this matters

GraphSAGE is a key inductive GNN architecture and directly supports reviewer/recommendation systems where new nodes appear over time.

Intuition

Instead of learning one embedding per node, GraphSAGE learns how to combine a node’s features with sampled neighbor features. That learned aggregator can be applied to unseen nodes.

Deep explanation

At each layer, sample/aggregate neighbor representations and combine them with the node’s current representation, often followed by nonlinear transformation/normalization. Mean, pooling and LSTM-style aggregators are possible. Sampling makes training scalable on large graphs, while inductive parameter sharing allows embeddings for new nodes if their features/neighborhood are available.

Math / formal view

h_v^(k)=σ(W^(k) · CONCAT(h_v^(k-1), AGG({h_u^(k-1):u∈N(v)})))

Worked example

For a new PR, its CodeBERT features plus learned transformations/graph context can place it near developers with relevant historical expertise without retraining a free embedding for that exact PR node.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement one GraphSAGE-style neighbor aggregation step with mean aggregation.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
X=np.array([[1.,0.],[0.,1.],[1.,1.]])
neighbors={0:[1,2],1:[0],2:[0]}
out=[]
for i in range(len(X)):
    agg=X[neighbors[i]].mean(0)
    out.append(np.concatenate([X[i],agg]))
out=np.stack(out)
print(out)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
W=np.array([[1.,0.],[0.,1.],[.5,0.],[0.,.5]])
H=np.maximum(0,out@W); print(H)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Refresh graph edges/features incrementally, bound neighbor sampling for latency, monitor cold-start quality and separate candidate generation from final ranking/business constraints.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert out.shape==(3,4)
assert H.shape==(3,2)

Common mistakes

  • Saying GraphSAGE requires every test node to exist during training.
  • Ignoring neighbor-sampling bias/variance.
  • Confusing graph structure with text similarity alone.

22.4

Link Prediction

highsummary
Roles: mle, ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Link prediction scores whether an edge should exist between two nodes. Candidate node embeddings are combined with a scoring function and trained against positive and negative edges.

What you must know

  • Negative sampling
  • Dot product/MLP scores
  • Temporal split
  • Ranking metrics

Why this matters

Link prediction is a natural formulation for reviewer recommendation, social connections and knowledge-graph completion.

Intuition

Learn node representations, then score whether a pair of nodes should have an edge. Training uses observed positive edges plus sampled negative pairs.

Deep explanation

Scores can be dot products, bilinear functions or neural decoders over node embeddings. Negative sampling matters because the number of non-edges is enormous and random negatives may be too easy. Temporal splits are important when predicting future links. Ranking evaluation often fits better than binary accuracy because the real task is choosing top candidates.

Math / formal view

s(u,v)=h_uᵀh_v (simple dot-product decoder); p(edge)=σ(s)

Worked example

For each PR, historical reviewer edges are positives. Candidate developers not reviewing that PR can be negatives, but avoid sampling impossible/inactive reviewers that make training unrealistically easy.

pr=np.array([1.,.2])
reviewers=np.array([[.9,.1],[0.,1.],[.5,.5],[-1.,0.]])
scores=reviewers@pr
rank=np.argsort(-scores)
print(rank,scores[rank])

recall_at_k=float(true_reviewer in rank[:k]); print('Recall@2',recall_at_k)

highsummary
Roles: ds, as, mle
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Deep explanation

A strong answer connects the formal idea to validation, data requirements and failure modes instead of treating the method as a recipe.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement one normalized GCN propagation step with NumPy.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
A=np.array([[0,1,1],[1,0,0],[1,0,0]],float)
X=np.array([[1.,0.],[0.,1.],[1.,1.]])
Ahat=A+np.eye(3); deg=Ahat.sum(1); D=np.diag(1/np.sqrt(deg)); S=D@Ahat@D
W=np.array([[1.,-.5],[.5,1.]])
H=np.maximum(0,S@X@W)
print(H)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API

22.8

Graph-level Prediction & Pooling

mediumsummary
Roles: as, mle
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

For graph-level tasks, node embeddings must be aggregated into a graph representation using mean/sum/max, attention or hierarchical pooling before prediction.

What you must know

  • Sum/mean pooling encode different size behavior.
  • Permutation invariance is required.
  • Pooling can bottleneck structural information.

Why this matters

Graph-level Prediction & Pooling is a standard part of a broad data/ML curriculum because it changes how models are selected, evaluated or operated in real systems.

Intuition

Sum/mean pooling encode different size behavior.

Deep explanation

For graph-level tasks, node embeddings must be aggregated into a graph representation using mean/sum/max, attention or hierarchical pooling before prediction. Permutation invariance is required. Pooling can bottleneck structural information. A strong answer connects the formal idea to validation, data requirements and failure modes instead of treating the method as a recipe.

Worked example

Predict molecular properties by message passing over atoms/bonds followed by graph pooling.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing the technique without checking whether its assumptions match the problem.
  • Optimizing an offline metric without checking realistic validation slices or operational constraints.

Likely follow-ups

  • When would you not use Graph-level Prediction & Pooling?
  • How would you validate or tune Graph-level Prediction & Pooling?

23.1

Neural Network Fundamentals

very highsummary
Roles: all, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A neural network composes linear transformations with nonlinear activations. Training adjusts parameters to minimize a loss, while intermediate layers learn representations useful for the task.

What you must know

  • Layers
  • Weights/biases
  • Activation
  • Loss/optimizer

Why this matters

Every DL interview expects you to explain a neural network from first principles, not just name PyTorch modules.

Intuition

A neural network repeatedly performs weighted combinations followed by nonlinear transformations. Training adjusts the weights so those transformations produce useful representations for the task.

Deep explanation

A feed-forward layer computes z=Wx+b and activation a=φ(z). Stacking linear layers without nonlinearities collapses to one linear transformation, so activations create expressive nonlinear functions. The final layer/loss depends on the task: logits plus cross-entropy for classification, continuous outputs with regression losses, etc. Parameters are learned by backpropagation and an optimizer over mini-batches.

Math / formal view

z^(l)=W^(l)a^(l-1)+b^(l) a^(l)=φ(z^(l))

Worked example

For image classification, early layers may detect local edges/textures while later layers combine them into task-specific patterns before the classifier head.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Train a tiny MLP end-to-end and inspect gradients.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import torch
x=torch.linspace(-2,2,200).unsqueeze(1); y=(x**2)
model=torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(1,32),torch.nn.ReLU(),torch.nn.Linear(32,1))
opt=torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(),lr=1e-2)
for _ in range(500):
    opt.zero_grad(); loss=torch.nn.functional.mse_loss(model(x),y); loss.backward(); opt.step()
print('loss',loss.item())
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
# Same pattern scales to real tasks: Dataset/DataLoader -> nn.Module -> loss -> optimizer.
print(model(torch.tensor([[1.5]])).item())
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

The architecture is only one part of a DL system; reproducible preprocessing, checkpoints, device/mixed-precision handling and monitoring are equally important.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert loss.item()<0.02
assert all(p.grad is not None for p in model.parameters())

Common mistakes

  • Saying neurons “think” independently rather than describing tensor operations.
  • Forgetting that outputs are usually logits before softmax/sigmoid loss handling.
  • Assuming more layers always improve performance.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why do we need nonlinear activations?
  • What is backpropagation?
  • How do you choose output activation/loss?
  • What causes overfitting in neural networks?

Production / system-design connection

The architecture is only one part of a DL system; reproducible preprocessing, checkpoints, device/mixed-precision handling and monitoring are equally important.

23.2

Backpropagation

very highsummary
Roles: all, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Backpropagation efficiently computes gradients by applying the chain rule from the loss backward through the computation graph. The optimizer then uses those gradients to update parameters.

What you must know

  • Forward vs backward
  • Chain rule
  • Autograd
  • Gradient accumulation

Why this matters

Interviewers want to know whether you understand what frameworks such as PyTorch automate.

Intuition

A forward pass computes the prediction and loss. Backprop starts at the loss and repeatedly applies the chain rule to compute how changing each parameter would change that loss.

Deep explanation

Backprop is reverse-mode automatic differentiation on a computation graph. It reuses intermediate derivatives so the gradient of a scalar loss with respect to millions of parameters is computed efficiently. The optimizer is separate: backprop gives gradients; SGD/Adam uses them.

Math / formal view

For z=wx+b and L=L(z): ∂L/∂w = (∂L/∂z)(∂z/∂w) = (∂L/∂z)x

Worked example

If w=2, x=3 and target=5, the model predicts 6. Backprop computes how changing w changes the squared error so the optimizer can move w downward.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Verify backpropagation against a hand-derived scalar gradient.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
# f(w)=(w*x-y)^2 -> df/dw=2*(w*x-y)*x
w,x,y=2.0,3.0,10.0
manual=2*(w*x-y)*x
print('manual',manual)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import torch
wt=torch.tensor(w,requires_grad=True); loss=(wt*x-y)**2; loss.backward()
print('autograd',wt.grad.item())
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

In production training, watch gradient norms and numerical stability; use clipping or mixed-precision scaling where appropriate.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(manual-wt.grad.item())<1e-6

Common mistakes

  • “Backprop updates weights.” Backprop computes gradients; the optimizer updates weights.
  • Forgetting optimizer.zero_grad() / gradient accumulation behavior in PyTorch.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does gradient descent move opposite the gradient?
  • What causes vanishing gradients?
  • What does detach() do?
  • Why is reverse mode efficient for neural nets?

Production / system-design connection

In production training, watch gradient norms and numerical stability; use clipping or mixed-precision scaling where appropriate.

23.3

Activation Functions

highsummary
Roles: mle, aie, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Nonlinear activations let deep networks represent nonlinear functions. ReLU-like functions are common in hidden layers; sigmoid/softmax are often used at outputs depending on the task.

What you must know

  • ReLU
  • Sigmoid
  • Softmax
  • Saturation

Why this matters

Activation functions determine gradient flow and expressive power. Interviewers often ask why deep networks need them and when specific activations fit.

Intuition

A linear layer only stretches/rotates space. A nonlinear activation bends it, so stacked layers can represent complex decision boundaries.

Deep explanation

ReLU=max(0,x) is cheap and avoids sigmoid-style saturation on positive inputs but can create dead units. Leaky ReLU/GELU/SiLU keep smoother or nonzero negative behavior. Sigmoid maps to (0,1) and is useful for binary probability outputs; softmax normalizes logits across mutually exclusive classes. The loss often expects raw logits, so applying sigmoid/softmax twice is a common bug.

Math / formal view

ReLU(x)=max(0,x) σ(x)=1/(1+e^{-x}) softmax(z_i)=e^{z_i}/Σ_j e^{z_j}

Worked example

For binary classification with BCEWithLogitsLoss, return one raw logit. The loss internally applies a stable sigmoid; manually applying sigmoid before it is unnecessary and can hurt numerical stability.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement common activations and inspect how they change values and gradients.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
x=np.array([-3.,-1.,0.,1.,3.])
relu=np.maximum(0,x)
sigmoid=1/(1+np.exp(-x))
tanh=np.tanh(x)
print('relu',relu,'sigmoid',sigmoid,'tanh',tanh)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import torch
t=torch.tensor(x,requires_grad=True)
y=torch.nn.functional.gelu(t).sum(); y.backward(); print(t.grad)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Use a small activation-comparison harness that plots outputs and gradient magnitudes for the data range your model actually sees; choose an activation based on optimization behavior, architecture conventions and numerical stability rather than fashion.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert relu[0]==0 and relu[-1]==3
assert np.all((sigmoid>0)&(sigmoid<1))

Common mistakes

  • Stacking linear layers without activations and expecting nonlinear capacity.
  • Applying softmax before CrossEntropyLoss or sigmoid before BCEWithLogitsLoss.
  • Saying ReLU has no drawbacks.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why can sigmoid cause vanishing gradients?
  • ReLU vs GELU?
  • When use softmax?
  • What are dead ReLUs?

Production / system-design connection

Match output activation/loss exactly between training and serving; logit/probability mismatches are a frequent deployment bug.

23.4

SGD, Momentum & Adam

very highsummary
Roles: mle, aie, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

SGD follows noisy mini-batch gradients; momentum smooths updates by accumulating velocity; Adam adapts step sizes using first and second gradient moments. No optimizer is universally best.

What you must know

  • Momentum
  • Adam moments
  • Weight decay
  • Learning-rate interaction

Why this matters

SGD vs Momentum vs Adam tests whether you understand how parameter updates are constructed and why optimization behavior differs.

Intuition

SGD follows the current noisy gradient. Momentum remembers recent directions to smooth oscillation. Adam additionally adapts the step scale per parameter using running gradient statistics.

Deep explanation

Momentum maintains an exponentially decayed velocity, accelerating consistent directions and damping zig-zag behavior. Adam tracks first and second moments of gradients with bias correction, often giving fast robust convergence. Weight decay should be understood carefully: AdamW decouples weight decay from Adam’s adaptive gradient step. Optimizer choice interacts with learning-rate schedule, batch size and generalization.

Math / formal view

Momentum: v_t=βv_{t-1}+g_t; θ←θ-ηv_t Adam: m_t=β₁m_{t-1}+(1-β₁)g_t; v_t=β₂v_{t-1}+(1-β₂)g_t²; update with bias-corrected m/√v

Worked example

If SGD oscillates across a narrow valley, momentum can average those alternating directions while preserving movement along the valley.

Quick code / pseudocode

opt=torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(),lr=3e-4,weight_decay=1e-2)

Common mistakes

  • Saying Adam is universally better than SGD.
  • Confusing L2 regularization with decoupled AdamW weight decay.
  • Comparing optimizers without retuning learning rates/schedules.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does momentum help?
  • Adam vs AdamW?
  • What does beta control?
  • Why can SGD generalize well in vision?

Production / system-design connection

Log optimizer configuration and scheduler state with checkpoints. Changing optimizer/schedule can invalidate comparisons even when architecture and data are unchanged.

23.5

Dropout, Weight Decay & Early Stopping

highsummary
Roles: mle, aie, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

These techniques reduce overfitting in different ways: dropout injects stochastic feature removal, weight decay penalizes large parameters, and early stopping limits training when validation stops improving.

What you must know

  • Train vs eval mode
  • L2/weight-decay nuance
  • Patience
  • Use validation metrics

Why this matters

Regularization questions test whether you can control generalization rather than only minimize training loss.

Intuition

Regularization deliberately makes fitting harder or noisier so the model cannot memorize every training detail and is pushed toward simpler, more robust behavior.

Deep explanation

Weight decay penalizes large weights; dropout randomly zeros activations during training; data augmentation expands invariances; early stopping limits optimization once validation stops improving. They address different failure modes and can interact. In modern networks, decoupled weight decay (AdamW) is often preferable to naive L2 with adaptive optimizers. Regularization strength should be selected on validation data.

Math / formal view

L_total = L_data + λ||w||² (L2-style) Dropout: h̃ = mask⊙h/(1-p) during training

Worked example

If training accuracy reaches 100% while validation stalls, first check leakage/split, then consider augmentation, weight decay, dropout or smaller capacity—not simply train longer.

Quick code / pseudocode

opt=torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(),lr=3e-4,weight_decay=1e-2)
layer=nn.Dropout(p=.2)

Common mistakes

  • Treating every generalization problem as “add dropout.”
  • Using validation/test interchangeably for early stopping.
  • Assuming L2 and AdamW weight decay are identical in adaptive optimization.

Likely follow-ups

  • Dropout train vs eval behavior?
  • What is early stopping patience?
  • L1 vs L2?
  • Why can augmentation regularize?

Production / system-design connection

Store the best validation checkpoint and exact preprocessing/augmentation config. Training-serving mismatch in dropout or normalization mode can destroy performance.

23.6

BatchNorm vs LayerNorm

highsummary
Roles: mle, aie, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

BatchNorm normalizes using batch statistics and is common in CNNs; LayerNorm normalizes features within each example and is standard in transformers. Their behavior at inference differs.

What you must know

  • Axes differ
  • Train/eval behavior
  • Batch-size sensitivity
  • Transformer use

Why this matters

BatchNorm vs LayerNorm is a common deep-learning question because they normalize along different dimensions and behave differently in training/inference.

Intuition

BatchNorm uses statistics across examples for each feature/channel. LayerNorm uses statistics within each example across its hidden features.

Deep explanation

BatchNorm normalizes activations using batch mean/variance and maintains running estimates for inference; small/non-iid batches can make estimates noisy. LayerNorm normalizes per token/sample and does not depend on other examples, making it natural for transformers and variable sequence lengths. Both include learned scale/shift parameters; neither simply “forces mean 0 forever.”

Math / formal view

BN: x̂=(x-μ_batch)/sqrt(σ²_batch+ε); y=γx̂+β LN: same form but μ,σ computed across chosen feature dimensions per sample

Worked example

A transformer token of dimension 768 can be LayerNormed across those 768 features independently of batch size, while BatchNorm would couple it to other batch examples.

Quick code / pseudocode

bn=nn.BatchNorm2d(64)
ln=nn.LayerNorm(768)

Common mistakes

  • Saying BatchNorm uses the current batch at inference.
  • Saying LayerNorm normalizes across the batch.
  • Forgetting model.eval() changes BatchNorm/Dropout behavior.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why LayerNorm in transformers?
  • What happens with tiny batches?
  • Pre-LN vs post-LN?
  • BatchNorm as regularization?

Production / system-design connection

Ensure training/eval modes are correct and saved running statistics are loaded. Distribution shifts can make BatchNorm statistics less representative.

23.7

Vanishing / Exploding Gradients

highsummary
Roles: mle, aie, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Repeated multiplication through deep networks can shrink or amplify gradients. Initialization, normalization, ReLU-like activations, residual connections and gradient clipping help depending on the architecture.

What you must know

  • Depth
  • Activation saturation
  • Residuals
  • Gradient clipping

Why this matters

Gradient pathologies explain why older deep networks were hard to train and motivate ReLU, residual connections, normalization and clipping.

Intuition

Backprop multiplies many local derivatives. If most are below 1, gradients shrink toward zero; if large, gradients can blow up.

Deep explanation

Sigmoid/tanh saturation can produce tiny derivatives; recurrent multiplication across long sequences intensifies the effect. Exploding gradients cause unstable updates/NaNs. Initialization preserves signal variance; ReLU-like activations reduce saturation; residual connections provide shorter identity paths; normalization stabilizes scales; gradient clipping caps extreme norms.

Math / formal view

For a chain, ∂L/∂h_0 = Π_l (∂h_l/∂h_{l-1}) · ∂L/∂h_L; repeated singular values <1 shrink and >1 amplify.

Worked example

If early layers show near-zero gradient norms while late layers learn, inspect saturation/initialization and consider residual/norm architecture rather than only increasing learning rate.

Quick code / pseudocode

torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)

Common mistakes

  • Using gradient clipping as a cure for every optimization problem.
  • Confusing vanishing gradients with overfitting.
  • Ignoring NaNs from data/loss even when gradients explode.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why do residual connections help?
  • Why ReLU helps vs sigmoid?
  • What does gradient clipping do?
  • How does initialization matter?

Production / system-design connection

Track gradient norms/NaNs in training telemetry and checkpoint before instability so long GPU runs can be diagnosed/resumed.

23.8

Debugging a Model That Will Not Learn

very highsummary
Roles: mle, aie, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Verify data and labels, then try to overfit a tiny batch. Inspect loss, outputs, gradients, learning rate, preprocessing and train/eval modes before changing architecture. Debug from simplest assumptions outward.

What you must know

  • Overfit tiny batch
  • Check labels
  • Inspect gradients
  • Establish simple baseline

Why this matters

Debugging questions reveal whether you can work independently when a model fails rather than randomly changing hyperparameters.

Intuition

Debug from the simplest possible failure outward: verify data and labels, then prove the model can overfit a tiny batch, then inspect gradients/loss/learning rate, then scale complexity.

Deep explanation

Check shapes, dtypes, normalization, label alignment and train/eval modes. Overfit one batch: if the model cannot drive training loss down, there is likely a pipeline, optimization or capacity bug. Inspect baseline loss, output ranges, gradient norms and which parameters receive gradients. Disable augmentation/regularization, simplify the model, compare against a trivial baseline, then reintroduce complexity one piece at a time.

Worked example

If binary classification loss stays near 0.693, inspect whether logits vary, labels are correct, gradients are nonzero and the optimizer actually owns the model parameters before increasing network depth.

Quick code / pseudocode

# Tiny-batch sanity test
x,y=next(iter(loader))
for _ in range(500):
    opt.zero_grad(); loss=criterion(model(x),y)
    loss.backward(); opt.step()
print(loss.item())

Common mistakes

  • Changing model architecture before verifying labels/data.
  • Debugging training and validation problems simultaneously.
  • Leaving dropout/augmentation on while trying to prove the pipeline can overfit a tiny batch.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why overfit one batch?
  • What if loss is NaN?
  • What if gradients are all zero?
  • Training loss decreases but validation worsens—what next?

Production / system-design connection

Capture reproducible configs, seeds, logs, sample inputs, checkpoints and environment versions so failures can be reproduced instead of debugged from memory.

24.1

CNN Fundamentals

very highsummary
Roles: mle, cv, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

CNNs exploit local spatial structure with shared filters. Early layers learn local edges/textures, while deeper layers combine them into larger receptive-field features.

What you must know

  • Kernel
  • Stride
  • Padding
  • Channels

Why this matters

CNNs remain foundational for vision and help explain locality, parameter sharing, receptive fields and why 2D vs 3D architectures behave differently.

Intuition

A convolution reuses the same small filter across locations, so the model learns patterns such as edges or textures regardless of where they appear.

Deep explanation

A convolution kernel slides across spatial dimensions, producing feature maps. Parameter sharing makes CNNs far more efficient than dense layers on images. Stride controls sampling; padding controls boundary/size behavior; dilation expands receptive field. Stacking layers builds hierarchical features and enlarges effective receptive field. Pooling/strided convolution reduce spatial resolution while increasing semantic abstraction.

Math / formal view

For 1D dimension: output = floor((N + 2P - D(K-1) - 1)/S + 1)

Worked example

A 3×3 RGB filter has 3×3×3 weights per output channel, and the same weights are applied at every image location, unlike a fully connected layer with separate weights per pixel.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Build a small CNN and verify spatial/channel shapes.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import torch
net=torch.nn.Sequential(
 torch.nn.Conv2d(1,8,3,padding=1),torch.nn.ReLU(),torch.nn.MaxPool2d(2),
 torch.nn.Conv2d(8,16,3,padding=1),torch.nn.ReLU(),torch.nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1),
 torch.nn.Flatten(),torch.nn.Linear(16,3))
x=torch.randn(4,1,64,64); print(net(x).shape)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
# Inspect feature map shape explicitly.
features=net[:3](x); print(features.shape)  # [4, 8, 32, 32]
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Vision pipelines must keep resize/crop/normalization identical between training and serving. Throughput depends heavily on resolution, batch size and device kernels.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert net(x).shape==(4,3)
assert features.shape==(4,8,32,32)

Common mistakes

  • Saying convolution is automatically translation invariant; it is more accurately translation equivariant before pooling/aggregation.
  • Ignoring channel dimensions.
  • Assuming a large theoretical receptive field means all pixels contribute equally in practice.

  • Why parameter sharing?
  • CNN vs ViT?
  • 2D vs 3D convolution?

Vision pipelines must keep resize/crop/normalization identical between training and serving. Throughput depends heavily on resolution, batch size and device kernels.

24.2

Receptive Field

highsummary
Roles: cv, mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A unit’s receptive field is the input region that can influence it. Deeper layers, larger kernels, stride and dilation increase receptive field and therefore spatial context.

What you must know

  • Effective vs theoretical
  • Stride
  • Dilation
  • Context vs detail

Why this matters

Receptive field explains how CNN features gather spatial context and why architecture choices affect fine details versus global structure.

Intuition

A feature in a deep layer “sees” a region of the original image. Deeper layers, larger kernels, stride and dilation increase that region.

Deep explanation

Theoretical receptive field accumulates through layers, but the effective receptive field may be smaller/nonuniform. Stride/pooling enlarge field faster while reducing spatial resolution. Dilation enlarges context without the same parameter count. For segmentation/reconstruction, balancing global context with local detail motivates skip connections and multi-scale architectures.

Worked example

Two stacked 3×3 stride-1 convolutions give a 5×5 theoretical receptive field; adding a stride-2 layer makes each subsequent feature cover input positions farther apart.

Common mistakes

  • Equating receptive field with kernel size of one layer.
  • Assuming every pixel inside the theoretical field contributes equally.
  • Increasing stride without considering lost detail.

Likely follow-ups

  • How does dilation affect receptive field?
  • Why use pooling/stride?
  • Why U-Net skip connections?
  • What is effective receptive field?

Production / system-design connection

For large images/3D patches, receptive field determines whether the model has enough contextual information; patch sizes and tiling overlap must match it.

24.3

Residual Networks

highsummary
Roles: cv, mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Residual connections learn a change relative to the input and create shorter gradient paths, making very deep networks easier to optimize.

What you must know

  • Skip connection
  • Identity mapping
  • Optimization benefit
  • Not just ensemble intuition

Why this matters

Residual networks are foundational because skip connections changed the trainability of very deep models and appear throughout modern architectures.

Intuition

Instead of forcing a block to learn a full transformation H(x), learn a residual F(x)=H(x)-x and add the input back: y=x+F(x).

Deep explanation

Identity shortcuts create short gradient paths and make it easier for a block to behave like identity if extra depth is unnecessary. When shapes differ, projection shortcuts can align dimensions. Residual connections do not eliminate all optimization issues but significantly improve signal/gradient propagation and are also used in transformers and diffusion U-Nets.

Math / formal view

y = x + F(x;W)

Worked example

If a residual branch initially outputs near zero, the block behaves approximately like identity, so adding depth does not necessarily destroy an already useful representation.

Quick code / pseudocode

def forward(self,x):
    return self.relu(x + self.block(x))

Common mistakes

  • Saying ResNet solves vanishing gradients completely.
  • Adding tensors with incompatible shapes without projection.
  • Confusing residual connections with DenseNet concatenation.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does identity help optimization?
  • What if channel count changes?
  • ResNet vs DenseNet?
  • Where else are residuals used?

Production / system-design connection

Residual backbones are mature/efficient; inference optimization often benefits from standard kernels and well-supported architectures.

24.4

U-Net & Segmentation

highsummary
Roles: cv, mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

U-Net combines an encoder that captures context with a decoder that restores spatial resolution, using skip connections to preserve fine localization information.

What you must know

  • Encoder/decoder
  • Skip connections
  • Pixel-wise prediction
  • Dice/IoU

Why this matters

U-Net is a standard encoder–decoder architecture for segmentation and reconstruction where both context and precise spatial localization matter.

Intuition

The encoder compresses spatial information while learning context; the decoder restores resolution. Skip connections copy high-resolution features from matching encoder stages to recover detail.

Deep explanation

Downsampling increases semantic context but loses exact position. U-Net concatenates or combines encoder features with decoder features at corresponding scales. Output heads depend on task: class logits per pixel/voxel for segmentation, image channels for reconstruction. 3D U-Nets extend convolutions to volumes but consume much more memory.

Worked example

In pore segmentation, deep features identify material context while shallow skip features preserve exact boundary locations that would be blurred by the bottleneck alone.

Quick code / pseudocode

# conceptual
enc1=block(x); enc2=block(pool(enc1))
dec1=up(enc2); out=block(torch.cat([dec1,enc1],dim=1))

Common mistakes

  • Calling U-Net skip connections residual additions by default; classic U-Net concatenates.
  • Ignoring output activation/loss for multi-class vs binary segmentation.
  • Using huge 3D volumes without patch/memory planning.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why skip connections?
  • U-Net vs autoencoder?
  • 2D vs 3D U-Net?
  • Which loss for imbalanced segmentation?

Production / system-design connection

Tiled inference needs overlap/blending to avoid seams. Monitor resolution/preprocessing and memory use carefully for 3D deployment.

24.5

2D vs 3D CNNs

very highsummary
Roles: cv, mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

2D convolutions model height and width, while 3D convolutions also model depth and can learn cross-slice volumetric context directly. The trade-off is dramatically higher memory and compute.

What you must know

  • Volumetric consistency
  • Parameter/activation cost
  • Patch-based training
  • Use-case fit

Why this matters

This comes up whenever your data has volumetric or temporal structure and is especially relevant to medical/scientific imaging.

Intuition

A 2D kernel sees local height×width neighborhoods. A 3D kernel also moves through depth, so it can learn relationships between neighboring slices instead of treating them independently.

Deep explanation

3D convolutions preserve volumetric context but activation memory grows quickly with depth and spatial resolution. For very large 3D volumes, common compromises are patches, anisotropic kernels, 2.5D multi-view models or hybrid architectures.

Math / formal view

2D kernel: kH×kW 3D kernel: kD×kH×kW

Worked example

For CT, MRI or materials volumes, a 3D-aware model can improve cross-slice consistency but may require patch-based training because full-volume activations exceed practical GPU memory.

Quick code / pseudocode

import torch.nn as nn
conv2d = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
conv3d = nn.Conv3d(1, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1)

Common mistakes

  • Saying a 3D CNN “directly creates 3D images” regardless of task—the architecture still needs a suitable input/output design.
  • Ignoring memory: 1024³ volumes are enormous.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is 2.5D?
  • How would you train on 1024³ volumes?
  • Why could plane-wise processing create inconsistency?

Production / system-design connection

Benchmark memory, throughput and accuracy. Patch extraction, overlap/blending and distributed inference may be required for large volumes.

24.6

Vision Transformers

highsummary
Roles: cv, aie, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A ViT splits an image into patches, embeds them as tokens, adds positional information and applies transformer blocks. Attention gives global interactions, while CNNs have stronger built-in locality.

What you must know

  • Patch embedding
  • Position
  • Self-attention
  • Data/compute considerations

Why this matters

Vision Transformers are common in modern vision and directly relevant to ViT-based tokenizers/embeddings.

Intuition

Split an image into patches, turn each patch into a token embedding, add positional information, then process the token sequence with transformer blocks.

Deep explanation

A patch embedding is often a strided convolution/linear projection. Self-attention gives global token interaction early, unlike CNN locality. ViTs usually need strong pretraining/data/regularization because they have weaker built-in image priors. CLS tokens or pooled tokens can summarize the image; dense tasks reshape/upsample token features.

Math / formal view

Number of tokens ≈ (H/P)(W/P) (+ optional CLS); attention cost scales O(N²) in token count.

Worked example

For 224×224 images with 16×16 patches, there are 14×14=196 patch tokens before optional special tokens.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Patchify a tiny image and inspect the token sequence a Vision Transformer would receive.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
img=np.arange(8*8).reshape(8,8)
patch=4
tokens=[]
for r in range(0,8,patch):
    for c in range(0,8,patch): tokens.append(img[r:r+patch,c:c+patch].reshape(-1))
tokens=np.stack(tokens)
print(tokens.shape)  # 4 patches x 16 pixels
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
# A real ViT linearly projects each flattened patch to hidden_dim, adds
# positional information, then applies Transformer encoder blocks.
hidden_dim=32
W=np.random.randn(tokens.shape[1],hidden_dim)
emb=tokens@W
print(emb.shape)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Turn patchification into a reusable preprocessing test: assert expected patch counts and embedding shapes for every supported image size, and fail early when an input cannot be partitioned as configured.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert tokens.shape==(4,16)
assert emb.shape==(4,32)

Common mistakes

  • Saying ViTs inherently know patch order without positional information.
  • Assuming attention is cheaper than CNNs at high resolution.
  • Treating CLS as mandatory for every vision task.

Likely follow-ups

  • CNN vs ViT?
  • Why patch size matters?
  • What does CLS token do?
  • How does attention cost scale?

Production / system-design connection

Resolution changes token count quadratically, affecting memory/latency. Preserve patching/normalization and consider efficient attention or hierarchical ViTs for large images.

24.7

PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS & FID

very highsummary
Roles: cv, genai, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

PSNR measures pixel-level fidelity, SSIM compares structural similarity, LPIPS uses deep features for perceptual similarity, and FID compares distributions of generated and real features. No single metric captures physical correctness.

What you must know

  • Pairwise vs distributional metrics
  • Metric/task alignment
  • Human/domain evaluation
  • Do not overinterpret FID

Why this matters

Image reconstruction/generation interviews often probe whether you know that pixel similarity, perceptual quality and distributional realism are different objectives.

Intuition

PSNR asks how close pixels are, SSIM compares local structural patterns, LPIPS compares deep perceptual features, and FID compares feature distributions across sets of images.

Deep explanation

PSNR is a logarithmic transform of MSE and rewards pixel fidelity. SSIM uses luminance/contrast/structure comparisons. LPIPS measures distance in pretrained deep feature spaces and often aligns better with perception. FID fits Gaussians to Inception features of real/generated image sets and compares their means/covariances; it is distribution-level and sensitive to sample size/domain mismatch. None guarantees physical correctness for scientific images.

Math / formal view

PSNR = 10 log10(MAX²/MSE) FID = ||μ_r-μ_g||² + Tr(Σ_r+Σ_g-2(Σ_rΣ_g)^{1/2})

Worked example

A slightly shifted reconstruction can have poor PSNR despite looking perceptually similar; a generative model can have good FID while failing to reproduce the exact input. Choose metrics to match the task.

Quick code / pseudocode

# PSNR from MSE for images normalized to [0,1]
import math
psnr = 10*math.log10(1.0/mse)

Common mistakes

  • Using FID for one image pair.
  • Interpreting high PSNR as proof of physical validity.
  • Comparing FID values computed with different feature pipelines/sample counts as if directly equivalent.

Likely follow-ups

  • PSNR vs SSIM?
  • Why can diffusion have low PSNR but useful samples?
  • What does FID actually compare?
  • What metric would you use for scientific microstructures?

Production / system-design connection

Define task-specific acceptance metrics alongside generic image metrics. For scientific/engineering vision, validate domain properties and downstream simulations, not aesthetics alone.

24.8

Super-resolution & Reconstruction

highsummary
Roles: cv, mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Super-resolution infers a higher-resolution signal from limited observations. The central tension is recovering detail without hallucinating unsupported structure, so downstream/domain validation is often essential.

What you must know

  • Paired vs unpaired data
  • Pixel vs perceptual objectives
  • Hallucination risk
  • 2D/3D consistency

Why this matters

Super-resolution/reconstruction interviews test whether you distinguish resolution enhancement, hallucination risk, paired/unpaired data and task-specific validation.

Intuition

The model maps a low-information input to a higher-resolution output. Because multiple high-resolution images can correspond to one low-resolution input, the problem is inherently ambiguous.

Deep explanation

Classical interpolation is deterministic and smooth but cannot invent missing high-frequency content. Supervised SR learns from aligned LR/HR pairs with pixel/perceptual/adversarial losses. Generative SR can create realistic texture but may hallucinate details. Scientific reconstruction therefore needs downstream structural/physical validation. 3D SR adds volumetric consistency and heavy compute constraints.

Worked example

A GAN can make SEM-like texture visually sharp while altering pore boundaries; PSNR/perceptual metrics alone cannot prove porosity correctness.

Common mistakes

  • Equating visually sharp output with ground-truth recovery.
  • Calling interpolation learned super-resolution.
  • Ignoring whether LR/HR pairs are aligned.

Likely follow-ups

  • Pixel loss vs perceptual loss?
  • Why can GAN SR lower PSNR?
  • How do you validate scientific SR?
  • 2D slice vs 3D model?

Production / system-design connection

Choose output acceptance metrics tied to downstream use, version preprocessing/scale factors, and use batch/GPU jobs for large 3D outputs.

  • Geometric/color transforms have domain assumptions.
  • Validation/test data should not receive stochastic training augmentation.

Why this matters

Intuition

Normalize consistently between train/serve.

Deep explanation

Image preprocessing standardizes model inputs; augmentation creates plausible label-preserving variation to improve generalization. Augmentations must respect task semantics—horizontal flips are not universally valid. Geometric/color transforms have domain assumptions. Validation/test data should not receive stochastic training augmentation. A strong answer connects the formal idea to validation, data requirements and failure modes instead of treating the method as a recipe.

Worked example

Use crop/color jitter for natural-image classification but avoid flips if left/right orientation carries medical meaning.

Common mistakes

25.1

Embeddings

very highsummary
Roles: aie, mle, ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Embeddings map discrete objects such as words, products or code into dense vectors where geometry captures learned relationships. They support similarity search, retrieval and neural-network inputs.

What you must know

  • Dense vectors
  • Cosine similarity
  • Contextual vs static
  • Dimensionality

Why this matters

Embeddings power semantic search, transformers, recommenders and graph/text systems. Interviewers expect both geometric intuition and awareness of retrieval limitations.

Intuition

An embedding maps an object—word, document, image, user, PR—into a vector so that useful relationships become geometric, often measured by cosine similarity or dot product.

Deep explanation

Embeddings can be learned through supervised, self-supervised or contrastive objectives. Similarity reflects the training objective and domain, not universal semantic truth. Vector magnitude may carry information for dot-product retrieval; cosine normalizes it away. Retrieval systems need compatible query/document encoders, appropriate chunking and an index such as HNSW/IVF for scale.

Math / formal view

cos(x,y) = (x·y)/(||x|| ||y||)

Worked example

CodeBERT maps PR text into vectors where semantically related software changes can be closer even when they do not share exact words, which is useful for reviewer recommendation.

Quick code / pseudocode

import numpy as np
def cosine(a,b):
    return a@b/(np.linalg.norm(a)*np.linalg.norm(b))

Common mistakes

  • Assuming nearest embedding means factually correct or causally related.
  • Mixing embeddings produced by incompatible models/spaces.
  • Using cosine and dot product interchangeably when vector norms differ.

Likely follow-ups

  • Cosine vs dot-product similarity?
  • How are embeddings trained?
  • What is an ANN index?
  • How do you evaluate embedding retrieval?

Production / system-design connection

Track embedding model/version with the index. Re-embedding can be expensive, and model changes can make old vectors incompatible with new queries.

25.2

Tokenization

highsummary
Roles: aie, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Tokenization converts text into a sequence of discrete token IDs. Subword methods balance vocabulary size and sequence length and must match the model’s training tokenizer exactly.

What you must know

  • BPE/WordPiece intuition
  • Special tokens
  • Unknown words
  • Tokenizer-model coupling

Why this matters

Tokenization defines the units language models operate on and directly affects context length, multilingual/code behavior and cost.

Intuition

A tokenizer converts raw text into integer token IDs from a finite vocabulary. Modern subword tokenizers balance whole-word efficiency with the ability to represent unseen words.

Deep explanation

BPE/WordPiece/Unigram learn subword vocabularies from corpora. The same visible string can tokenize differently across models. Token count—not character/word count—drives context usage and inference cost. Special tokens encode boundaries/control signals. Byte-level schemes guarantee coverage but may use more tokens for some languages/domains.

Worked example

A rare technical identifier may split into many subword tokens, consuming context and potentially weakening semantic representation compared with common words.

Quick code / pseudocode

tokens=tokenizer("microstructure reconstruction", return_tensors="pt")
print(tokens.input_ids)

Common mistakes

  • Assuming one token equals one word.
  • Using a tokenizer from a different model than the embedding/LLM weights.
  • Hard-coding character limits when the real constraint is tokens.

Likely follow-ups

  • BPE intuition?
  • Why special tokens?
  • Why tokenization differs by language?
  • How does token count affect cost?

Production / system-design connection

Estimate/request limits in tokens, version tokenizer with the model, and handle truncation/chunking explicitly.

25.3

Language Modeling & Next-token Prediction

highsummary
Roles: aie, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A causal language model estimates the probability of each next token conditioned on previous tokens and trains using cross-entropy over sequences. Generation repeatedly samples or selects from the predicted distribution.

What you must know

  • Autoregression
  • Cross-entropy
  • Teacher forcing intuition
  • Sampling

Why this matters

Next-token prediction is the central training objective behind decoder-only LLMs and connects probabilities, cross-entropy, perplexity and inference.

Intuition

Given previous tokens, predict a probability distribution for the next token. Repeating this process autoregressively produces text.

Deep explanation

Training uses teacher forcing: the model sees ground-truth previous tokens and minimizes token-level cross-entropy. The likelihood of a sequence factorizes as a product of conditional next-token probabilities. At inference, the model feeds generated tokens back into context and samples/decodes from logits. Exposure to broad data plus scale produces useful representations/behaviors, but the objective optimizes predictive likelihood—not truthfulness.

Math / formal view

p(x_1...x_T)=Π_t p(x_t | x_{<t}) NLL = -Σ_t log p(x_t|x_{<t}) Perplexity = exp(mean NLL per token)

Worked example

If the correct next token gets probability 0.8, its loss is -log(0.8); if probability is 0.01, the loss is much larger.

Quick code / pseudocode

# CrossEntropyLoss over shifted logits/labels is the common training pattern
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits[:, :-1].reshape(-1,V), ids[:,1:].reshape(-1))

Common mistakes

  • Saying next-token training explicitly teaches factual truth or reasoning steps.
  • Confusing teacher forcing with autoregressive inference.
  • Comparing perplexity across incompatible tokenizers without caution.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is perplexity?
  • Why causal mask?
  • Teacher forcing?
  • Why can next-token prediction lead to broad capabilities?

Production / system-design connection

Inference cost depends on context/prefill plus token-by-token decoding; KV cache avoids recomputing all prior attention states each step.

mediumsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

What you must know

  • Stemming is heuristic; lemmatization uses linguistic forms.
  • Do not normalize IDs/code like prose.

Why this matters

Text Normalization, Stemming & Lemmatization appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Tokenization requirements depend on downstream model.

Deep explanation

Text normalization standardizes forms before classical NLP/search, but aggressive normalization can destroy meaning for names, code, languages or modern subword models. Stemming is heuristic; lemmatization uses linguistic forms. Do not normalize IDs/code like prose. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Lowercase general prose for a classical model but preserve case/symbols for code identifiers where they carry meaning.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
  • Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.

Likely follow-ups

Speech & Audio Transformers: Spectrograms and ASR

mediumsummary
Roles: aie, mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Audio models typically convert a waveform into time-frequency features such as log-Mel spectrograms, then use an encoder or encoder-decoder model to classify audio or generate text. Whisper is a well-known transformer encoder-decoder trained for multilingual speech recognition, translation and language identification.

What you must know

  • waveform → spectrogram
  • temporal sequence
  • encoder / encoder-decoder
  • ASR

Why this matters

Audio is an important modality in multimodal AI and introduces sequence-length, sampling-rate and streaming constraints that differ from text/images.

Intuition

A spectrogram turns sound into an image-like map of frequency over time; the model then learns patterns across that temporal-frequency representation.

Deep explanation

ASR systems normalize/resample audio and create acoustic features such as log-Mel spectrograms. Transformer encoders model the acoustic sequence; sequence-to-sequence decoders generate text tokens. Other architectures use CTC. Streaming ASR adds chunking, context windows and latency trade-offs.

Worked example

A 30-second audio clip is resampled, converted to log-Mel features, encoded, and decoded autoregressively into transcript tokens.

Common mistakes

  • Treating raw audio samples as equivalent to text tokens without discussing preprocessing/feature representation.
  • Ignoring word-error rate and streaming latency in ASR evaluation.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is WER?
  • CTC vs encoder-decoder ASR?
  • How would you stream inference?

Production / system-design connection

Track word-error rate by accent/noise/domain, real-time factor, chunk latency and audio-quality failures; audio privacy/PII can be especially sensitive.

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Convert a waveform into an STFT magnitude spectrogram.

import numpy as np
fs=16000; t=np.arange(fs)/fs
x=np.sin(2*np.pi*440*t)+.3*np.sin(2*np.pi*880*t)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API

mag=np.abs(Z)

26.4

Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC)

mediumsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

CTC trains sequence models when input frames are much longer than output labels and exact alignments are unknown. It sums over valid alignments using blank/repeated-token rules.

What you must know

  • Alignment is monotonic.
  • Blank token enables flexible timing.
  • Decoding can be greedy or beam search.

Why this matters

Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Alignment is monotonic.

Deep explanation

CTC trains sequence models when input frames are much longer than output labels and exact alignments are unknown. It sums over valid alignments using blank/repeated-token rules. Blank token enables flexible timing. Decoding can be greedy or beam search. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Map hundreds of acoustic frames to a much shorter character sequence without frame-level transcription labels.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
  • Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.

Likely follow-ups

Word Error Rate counts substitutions, deletions and insertions relative to reference word count. It is interpretable but can hide semantic differences and depends on text normalization conventions. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

27.1

Self-Attention: Q, K, V

very highsummary
Roles: aie, mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Self-attention lets each token build a context-dependent representation by comparing its query with other tokens’ keys and taking a weighted combination of their values.

What you must know

  • Scaled dot product
  • Softmax weights
  • Multi-head attention
  • Quadratic sequence cost

Why this matters

Attention is the central operation behind modern transformers and many multimodal/generative systems.

Intuition

Think of each token asking a question (query), advertising what it contains (key), and carrying information to share (value). Query–key similarity determines how much of each value is mixed into the output.

Deep explanation

For matrices Q, K and V, scaled dot-product attention computes QKᵀ/√d, applies softmax row-wise, and multiplies by V. Multiple heads learn different projection subspaces. Causal language models additionally mask future positions.

Math / formal view

Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V

Worked example

In a sentence, the representation of “bank” can attend differently to “river” versus “loan”, producing context-dependent meaning.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement scaled dot-product self-attention with explicit tensor shapes.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import torch, math
B,T,D=2,4,8
x=torch.randn(B,T,D); Wq=torch.randn(D,D); Wk=torch.randn(D,D); Wv=torch.randn(D,D)
Q,K,V=x@Wq,x@Wk,x@Wv
scores=Q@K.transpose(-2,-1)/math.sqrt(D)
weights=scores.softmax(-1); out=weights@V
print(Q.shape,scores.shape,out.shape)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from torch.nn.functional import scaled_dot_product_attention
out2=scaled_dot_product_attention(Q,K,V)
print(out2.shape)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Long contexts create memory/latency pressure; serving systems use KV caches, efficient attention kernels and sometimes alternative architectures.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert torch.allclose(weights.sum(-1),torch.ones(B,T),atol=1e-5)
assert out.shape==(B,T,D)

Common mistakes

  • Saying attention “finds the most important word” as if it were one fixed interpretation.
  • Forgetting the √d scaling or causal mask.
  • Assuming attention weights are guaranteed explanations.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why multi-head attention?
  • Why is attention O(n²) in sequence length?
  • What are cross-attention and self-attention?
  • What is KV caching?

Production / system-design connection

Long contexts create memory/latency pressure; serving systems use KV caches, efficient attention kernels and sometimes alternative architectures.

27.2

Transformer Architecture

very highsummary
Roles: aie, mle, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Transformers combine attention, feed-forward networks, residual connections and normalization. Encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder variants serve different tasks.

What you must know

  • Attention block
  • MLP
  • Residual/LayerNorm
  • Causal mask

Why this matters

Transformers are central to modern NLP, vision and generative AI; you should be able to explain the block, not only self-attention.

Intuition

Each token first gathers context through attention, then independently passes through a feed-forward network. Residual connections and normalization stabilize deep stacks.

Deep explanation

A transformer block typically contains multi-head attention, position-wise feed-forward layers, residual connections and normalization. Attention projects hidden states to Q/K/V, computes compatibility and mixes values. Multiple heads learn different subspaces. Encoders use bidirectional attention; autoregressive decoders apply causal masks. Positional information is required because plain attention has no inherent sequence order.

Math / formal view

Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V FFN(x)=W₂ φ(W₁x+b₁)+b₂

Worked example

In a causal language model, token t can attend to positions ≤t but not future tokens; the causal mask enforces next-token prediction semantics.

Quick code / pseudocode

# PyTorch concept
layer = torch.nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d_model=512,nhead=8,batch_first=True)

Common mistakes

  • Explaining a transformer as “just attention” and omitting FFN/residual/norm.
  • Forgetting causal masking in decoder-only language models.
  • Saying attention gives order without positional information.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why divide by sqrt(d_k)?
  • Encoder vs decoder-only transformer?
  • What does multi-head attention buy?
  • Why LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm?

Production / system-design connection

Transformer inference cost grows with sequence length; batching, KV cache, quantization and context management are major serving concerns.

27.3

BERT vs GPT-style Models

highsummary
Roles: aie, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

BERT-style models are typically encoder-only and learn bidirectional contextual representations; GPT-style models are decoder-only and autoregressively predict the next token. Their pretraining objectives drive different strengths.

What you must know

  • Masked LM vs causal LM
  • Encoding vs generation
  • Fine-tuning
  • Context direction

Why this matters

BERT vs GPT tests whether you understand encoder-style bidirectional representation learning versus causal autoregressive generation.

Intuition

BERT-style encoders can look both left and right to understand a token in context. GPT-style decoder-only models predict the next token using only earlier tokens.

Deep explanation

BERT is pretrained with masked-token objectives and is strong for embeddings/classification/extraction with task heads. GPT-style models use causal masks and next-token prediction, naturally supporting generation and in-context prompting. Modern systems blur categories with encoder-decoder and instruction-tuned variants, so choose based on task rather than brand.

Worked example

For semantic classification of a complete PR description, an encoder such as CodeBERT/BERT can produce contextual features. For generating an explanation, a causal LLM is more natural.

Common mistakes

  • Calling BERT generative in the same autoregressive sense as GPT.
  • Saying GPT has no bidirectional information at all—later tokens integrate all earlier context, but cannot see future tokens during causal prediction.
  • Assuming one family always has better embeddings.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is causal masking?
  • Why masked language modeling?
  • Encoder-decoder transformer use case?
  • How would you get sentence embeddings from BERT?

Production / system-design connection

Encoder models are often cheaper for embeddings/classification; generative LLMs add latency/cost and should be used only when generation/reasoning is needed.
